quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 1 · Easy (Beginner Foundation & Terminal Orientation)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 10 · Beginner Orientation] Before pasting Page 10's one-liner (`Page 10: Loading the Synopsys EDA Toolchain Envi`), which terminal environment should you paste into, and what happens immediately after you press `Return`?
options: A) Paste it into Microsoft Word or a browser URL bar.

B) Paste it into your clean local MacBook Air Terminal window (`huynguyen@MacBook-Air ~ %`, running `zsh`); `snap_step` executes the command, verifies the output against Page 10's expected result, and either unlocks the green Post-Lab Learning view or provides a 1-click Auto-Debug Fix command if an error occurs.
C) Paste it into a disconnected terminal window showing `Broken pipe` without reconnecting.
D) Reboot the laptop after every single command.
quiz_questions.hint: Check the environment badge on Page 10: is this step running locally on your MacBook Air or on the remote SFSU Linux EDA server (`mahmoodi`), and how does `snap_step` talk back to the website?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Shell commands must be pasted into an active UNIX terminal emulator (`Terminal.app` or `XQuartz xterm`), not a word processor or browser address bar.

Correct! Pasting into your clean local MacBook Air Terminal window (`huynguyen@MacBook-Air ~ %`, running `zsh`) runs the command inside `snap_step`, which automatically checks the exit code and required markers and updates your live `:8788` web console!

Incorrect — A terminal showing `client_loop: send disconnect: Broken pipe` has lost its SSH connection; you must either use your clean local terminal window or run the Step 0 Auto-Connect command first.
Incorrect — You never need to reboot between pages; `snap_step` preserves your state continuously from Page 1 to Page 100.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) Page 10 runs in your clean local MacBook Air Terminal window (`huynguyen@MacBook-Air ~ %`, running `zsh`). Pressing `Return` triggers `snap_step`, which logs the output, captures the screenshot, and sends real-time verification telemetry to the website.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 2 · Easy-Medium (Hands-On Command Mechanics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 10 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 10's combined one-liner, why do we execute `cd ~/me_asic_new_v1` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Executes sequential step operation: `cd ~/me_asic_new_v1` Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 10's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `cd ~/me_asic_new_v1` performs: Executes sequential step operation: `cd ~/me_asic_new_v1` And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 10's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Lecture 1 & EDA Server Architecture)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 10 · Workstation & X11 Flow] Why must we use `ssh -Y` (trusted X11 forwarding) inside an active XQuartz session when connecting to `926784856@mahmoodi.rcc.at.sfsu.edu`?
options: A) Because Verilog files cannot be edited without a GUI.

B) Because Synopsys Verdi (`verdi`) and Fusion Compiler GUI (`fc_shell -gui`) render X11 graphics on the remote Linux server and forward the window draw calls over SSH to your MacBook's XQuartz display (`localhost:10.0`).
C) Because `ssh -Y` doubles the clock frequency of the Motion Estimator.
D) Because GitHub requires XQuartz to push commits.
quiz_questions.hint: Think about where the Synopsys EDA binaries (`verdi`, `fc_shell`) physically execute (on SFSU's Linux server) versus where your physical monitor is located (on your MacBook Air).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Verilog source files are plain ASCII text and can be edited in terminal editors (`vim`, `nano`, `cat << 'EOF'`) without any GUI.
Correct! Remote Linux EDA tools are X11 clients; `ssh -Y` sets `DISPLAY=localhost:10.0` on `mahmoodi` and tunnels window drawing commands over SSH to your MacBook's XQuartz X11 server.
Incorrect — Clock frequency (`520 MHz`) is defined in the Verilog testbench (`#0.9615`) and SDC constraints (`create_clock -period 1.923`), not by SSH flags.
Incorrect — `git push` uses HTTPS or SSH port 22 and never uses X11 display forwarding.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) Remote Linux EDA tools (`verdi`, `fc_shell -gui`) are X11 clients. `ssh -Y` sets `DISPLAY=localhost:10.0` on `mahmoodi` and securely tunnels X11 GUI frames back to XQuartz on your MacBook Air.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (V1→V9 Top-Level ASIC Port Boundary)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 10 · Rubric & Top-Level Boundary] Why are the frame-buffer memories `RMEM` (256x8) and `SMEM` (1024x8) instantiated inside the testbench (`top_tb.v`) rather than inside the synthesizable `top.v` module?
options: A) To measure and synthesize only the 16-PE systolic motion-estimator core + controller (449 FFs, 0 SRAM macros, 7,854.4 um^2) rather than bloating core area >10x by synthesizing 1,280 bytes (10,240 bits) of frame-buffer storage into standard-cell flip-flops.
B) Because `RMEM` uses analog voltages that cannot be simulated in VCS.
C) Because Synopsys VCS cannot simulate modules with memory ports.
D) Because `AddressR` is an input port of `top.v`.
quiz_questions.hint: Calculate how many D flip-flops would be created if `256 x 8` + `1024 x 8` bits of memory were synthesized directly into standard cells (`1,280 bytes * 8 bits/byte = 10,240 FFs`) vs. the 449 FFs in the 16-PE datapath.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! Synthesizing 1,280 bytes of memory as flip-flops would add 10,240 DFFs (more than 22x our 449-FF datapath!). Keeping `RMEM`/`SMEM` in the testbench isolates the pure 16-PE Motion Estimator core.
Incorrect — Both `RMEM` and `SMEM` are pure digital 8-bit behavioral arrays (`reg [7:0] RMEM[0:255]`).
Incorrect — VCS simulates memory ports effortlessly; the separation is strictly an ASIC synthesis boundary decision.
Incorrect — `AddressR[7:0]` is an OUTPUT port driven by `top.v` (`control.v`) to address the external `RMEM`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `top.v` outputs `AddressR[7:0]`, `AddressS1[9:0]`, `AddressS2[9:0]` and receives `R[7:0]`, `S1[7:0]`, `S2[7:0]` from external memory, keeping the synthesized 14nm core compact (`125.07 x 62.80 um`, 8,230 cells, 449 FFs, 0 SRAM macros).

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (520 MHz Timing Budget & Lecture 1 Economics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 10 · Advanced ASIC Specification] Our Motion Estimator targets `f_clk = 520 MHz` in Synopsys `SAED14nm` FinFET with external `RMEM`/`SMEM` memories and `set_input_delay 0.50 ns` / `set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.30 ns`. If internal DFF setup time is `t_setup = 0.05 ns`, what is the maximum combinational delay allowed on the input path from port `R[7:0]` into `pe0`?
options: B) 1.073 ns (since T_clk = 1/520 MHz = 1.923 ns, and T_logic,max = 1.923 - 0.50 [input_delay] - 0.30 [uncertainty] - 0.05 [t_setup] = 1.073 ns)
quiz_questions.hint: Apply the Midterm Q7 Input-to-Register formula: `T_logic,max = T_clk - set_input_delay - T_uncertainty - T_setup`, where `T_clk = 1000 / 520 = 1.923 ns`.
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `1.923 ns` is the full clock period `T_clk` before subtracting external input delay (`0.50 ns`), clock uncertainty (`0.30 ns`), and flip-flop setup time (`0.05 ns`).
Correct! By Midterm Q7's Input-to-Register equation: `T_logic,max = 1.923 - 0.50 - 0.30 - 0.05 = 1.073 ns`.
Incorrect — `1.423 ns` subtracts `input_delay (0.50 ns)` but forgets `clock_uncertainty (0.30 ns)` and `t_setup (0.05 ns)`.
Incorrect — `0.500 ns` is the external input arrival delay (`set_input_delay`), not the remaining internal logic budget.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) First compute `T_clk = 1 / (520 x 10^6) = 1.923 ns`. Then subtract external arrival delay (`0.50 ns`), setup uncertainty (`0.30 ns`), and DFF setup time (`0.05 ns`): `1.923 - 0.50 - 0.30 - 0.05 = 1.073 ns`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 1 · Easy (Beginner Foundation & Terminal Orientation)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 11 · Beginner Orientation] Before pasting Page 11's one-liner (`Page 11: Transferring Files Between Your New Mac`), which terminal environment should you paste into, and what happens immediately after you press `Return`?
options: A) Paste it into Microsoft Word or a browser URL bar.

B) Paste it into your clean local MacBook Air Terminal window (`huynguyen@MacBook-Air ~ %`, running `zsh`); `snap_step` executes the command, verifies the output against Page 11's expected result, and either unlocks the green Post-Lab Learning view or provides a 1-click Auto-Debug Fix command if an error occurs.
C) Paste it into a disconnected terminal window showing `Broken pipe` without reconnecting.
D) Reboot the laptop after every single command.
quiz_questions.hint: Check the environment badge on Page 11: is this step running locally on your MacBook Air or on the remote SFSU Linux EDA server (`mahmoodi`), and how does `snap_step` talk back to the website?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Shell commands must be pasted into an active UNIX terminal emulator (`Terminal.app` or `XQuartz xterm`), not a word processor or browser address bar.

Correct! Pasting into your clean local MacBook Air Terminal window (`huynguyen@MacBook-Air ~ %`, running `zsh`) runs the command inside `snap_step`, which automatically checks the exit code and required markers and updates your live `:8788` web console!

Incorrect — A terminal showing `client_loop: send disconnect: Broken pipe` has lost its SSH connection; you must either use your clean local terminal window or run the Step 0 Auto-Connect command first.
Incorrect — You never need to reboot between pages; `snap_step` preserves your state continuously from Page 1 to Page 100.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) Page 11 runs in your clean local MacBook Air Terminal window (`huynguyen@MacBook-Air ~ %`, running `zsh`). Pressing `Return` triggers `snap_step`, which logs the output, captures the screenshot, and sends real-time verification telemetry to the website.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 2 · Easy-Medium (Hands-On Command Mechanics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 11 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 11's combined one-liner, why do we execute `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/8bit ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 11's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/8bit ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 11's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Lecture 1 & EDA Server Architecture)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 11 · Workstation & X11 Flow] Why must we use `ssh -Y` (trusted X11 forwarding) inside an active XQuartz session when connecting to `926784856@mahmoodi.rcc.at.sfsu.edu`?
options: A) Because Verilog files cannot be edited without a GUI.

B) Because Synopsys Verdi (`verdi`) and Fusion Compiler GUI (`fc_shell -gui`) render X11 graphics on the remote Linux server and forward the window draw calls over SSH to your MacBook's XQuartz display (`localhost:10.0`).
C) Because `ssh -Y` doubles the clock frequency of the Motion Estimator.
D) Because GitHub requires XQuartz to push commits.
quiz_questions.hint: Think about where the Synopsys EDA binaries (`verdi`, `fc_shell`) physically execute (on SFSU's Linux server) versus where your physical monitor is located (on your MacBook Air).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Verilog source files are plain ASCII text and can be edited in terminal editors (`vim`, `nano`, `cat << 'EOF'`) without any GUI.
Correct! Remote Linux EDA tools are X11 clients; `ssh -Y` sets `DISPLAY=localhost:10.0` on `mahmoodi` and tunnels window drawing commands over SSH to your MacBook's XQuartz X11 server.
Incorrect — Clock frequency (`520 MHz`) is defined in the Verilog testbench (`#0.9615`) and SDC constraints (`create_clock -period 1.923`), not by SSH flags.
Incorrect — `git push` uses HTTPS or SSH port 22 and never uses X11 display forwarding.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) Remote Linux EDA tools (`verdi`, `fc_shell -gui`) are X11 clients. `ssh -Y` sets `DISPLAY=localhost:10.0` on `mahmoodi` and securely tunnels X11 GUI frames back to XQuartz on your MacBook Air.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (V1→V9 Top-Level ASIC Port Boundary)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 11 · Rubric & Top-Level Boundary] Why are the frame-buffer memories `RMEM` (256x8) and `SMEM` (1024x8) instantiated inside the testbench (`top_tb.v`) rather than inside the synthesizable `top.v` module?
options: A) To measure and synthesize only the 16-PE systolic motion-estimator core + controller (449 FFs, 0 SRAM macros, 7,854.4 um^2) rather than bloating core area >10x by synthesizing 1,280 bytes (10,240 bits) of frame-buffer storage into standard-cell flip-flops.
B) Because `RMEM` uses analog voltages that cannot be simulated in VCS.
C) Because Synopsys VCS cannot simulate modules with memory ports.
D) Because `AddressR` is an input port of `top.v`.
quiz_questions.hint: Calculate how many D flip-flops would be created if `256 x 8` + `1024 x 8` bits of memory were synthesized directly into standard cells (`1,280 bytes * 8 bits/byte = 10,240 FFs`) vs. the 449 FFs in the 16-PE datapath.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! Synthesizing 1,280 bytes of memory as flip-flops would add 10,240 DFFs (more than 22x our 449-FF datapath!). Keeping `RMEM`/`SMEM` in the testbench isolates the pure 16-PE Motion Estimator core.
Incorrect — Both `RMEM` and `SMEM` are pure digital 8-bit behavioral arrays (`reg [7:0] RMEM[0:255]`).
Incorrect — VCS simulates memory ports effortlessly; the separation is strictly an ASIC synthesis boundary decision.
Incorrect — `AddressR[7:0]` is an OUTPUT port driven by `top.v` (`control.v`) to address the external `RMEM`.

Correct! Pasting into your clean local MacBook Air Terminal window (`huynguyen@MacBook-Air ~ %`, running `zsh`) runs the command inside `snap_step`, which automatically checks the exit code and required markers and updates your live `:8788` web console!

Incorrect — A terminal showing `client_loop: send disconnect: Broken pipe` has lost its SSH connection; you must either use your clean local terminal window or run the Step 0 Auto-Connect command first.

quiz_questions.q: [Page 12 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 12's combined one-liner, why do we execute `cd ~/me_asic_new_v1` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Executes sequential step operation: `cd ~/me_asic_new_v1` Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 12's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `cd ~/me_asic_new_v1` performs: Executes sequential step operation: `cd ~/me_asic_new_v1` And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 12's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.q: [Page 12 · Rubric & Top-Level Boundary] Why are the frame-buffer memories `RMEM` (256x8) and `SMEM` (1024x8) instantiated inside the testbench (`top_tb.v`) rather than inside the synthesizable `top.v` module?
options: A) To measure and synthesize only the 16-PE systolic motion-estimator core + controller (449 FFs, 0 SRAM macros, 7,854.4 um^2) rather than bloating core area >10x by synthesizing 1,280 bytes (10,240 bits) of frame-buffer storage into standard-cell flip-flops.
B) Because `RMEM` uses analog voltages that cannot be simulated in VCS.
C) Because Synopsys VCS cannot simulate modules with memory ports.
D) Because `AddressR` is an input port of `top.v`.
quiz_questions.hint: Calculate how many D flip-flops would be created if `256 x 8` + `1024 x 8` bits of memory were synthesized directly into standard cells (`1,280 bytes * 8 bits/byte = 10,240 FFs`) vs. the 449 FFs in the 16-PE datapath.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! Synthesizing 1,280 bytes of memory as flip-flops would add 10,240 DFFs (more than 22x our 449-FF datapath!). Keeping `RMEM`/`SMEM` in the testbench isolates the pure 16-PE Motion Estimator core.
Incorrect — Both `RMEM` and `SMEM` are pure digital 8-bit behavioral arrays (`reg [7:0] RMEM[0:255]`).
Incorrect — VCS simulates memory ports effortlessly; the separation is strictly an ASIC synthesis boundary decision.
Incorrect — `AddressR[7:0]` is an OUTPUT port driven by `top.v` (`control.v`) to address the external `RMEM`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `top.v` outputs `AddressR[7:0]`, `AddressS1[9:0]`, `AddressS2[9:0]` and receives `R[7:0]`, `S1[7:0]`, `S2[7:0]` from external memory, keeping the synthesized 14nm core compact (`125.07 x 62.80 um`, 8,230 cells, 449 FFs, 0 SRAM macros).

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (520 MHz Timing Budget & Lecture 1 Economics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 12 · Advanced ASIC Specification] Our Motion Estimator targets `f_clk = 520 MHz` in Synopsys `SAED14nm` FinFET with external `RMEM`/`SMEM` memories and `set_input_delay 0.50 ns` / `set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.30 ns`. If internal DFF setup time is `t_setup = 0.05 ns`, what is the maximum combinational delay allowed on the input path from port `R[7:0]` into `pe0`?
options: B) 1.073 ns (since T_clk = 1/520 MHz = 1.923 ns, and T_logic,max = 1.923 - 0.50 [input_delay] - 0.30 [uncertainty] - 0.05 [t_setup] = 1.073 ns)
quiz_questions.hint: Apply the Midterm Q7 Input-to-Register formula: `T_logic,max = T_clk - set_input_delay - T_uncertainty - T_setup`, where `T_clk = 1000 / 520 = 1.923 ns`.
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `1.923 ns` is the full clock period `T_clk` before subtracting external input delay (`0.50 ns`), clock uncertainty (`0.30 ns`), and flip-flop setup time (`0.05 ns`).
Correct! By Midterm Q7's Input-to-Register equation: `T_logic,max = 1.923 - 0.50 - 0.30 - 0.05 = 1.073 ns`.
Incorrect — `1.423 ns` subtracts `input_delay (0.50 ns)` but forgets `clock_uncertainty (0.30 ns)` and `t_setup (0.05 ns)`.
Incorrect — `0.500 ns` is the external input arrival delay (`set_input_delay`), not the remaining internal logic budget.

trap_notes: BLUE:Why Block-Matching Saves Video Bandwidth:
Instead of transmitting all 256 raw pixel bytes of R, the encoder transmits only the 2-byte motion vector
(motionX, motionY) pointing to the closest matching 16x16 block in the previous frame plus tiny residuals!
code_block: // Mathematical Definition (Lecture Notes Chapter 10, Section 10.4, Equation on p. 144):
// For each candidate offset (i, j) with i in 0..15 and j in 0..15:
// Best match is the candidate (i*, j*) that minimizes D(i, j).
// --- Interactive Hardware Verification of This Architectural Step on mahmoodi ---

TERM_SFSU: [926784856@mahmoodi me_asic_new_v1]$ tcsh -c 'source ./scripts/synopsys_setup.tcl; vcs -full64 -sverilog -debug_access+all rtl/16bit/top.v tb/16bit/top_tb_direct.v -o simv_check && ./simv_check'
OUT_OK:    Cycle 256 (0x0100): CompStart=1, PEready=0x0001 | Cycle 4111 (0x100F): completed=1, BestDist=16'h0000
// --- Comparing 8-Bit Baseline (rtl/8bit/top.v) vs. 16-Bit Non-Saturating Upgrade (rtl/16bit/top.v) ---
01: // In 8-bit PE:  {Carry, AccumulateIn} = Accumulate + difference; if (Carry == 1) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;
02: // In 16-bit PE: AccumulateIn = Accumulate + {8'd0, difference};  // Exact sum up to 256*255 = 65,280 (16'hFF00)
03: // In 8-bit Control:  reg [11:0] count; // Wraps to 0 at cycle 4096 -> resets BestDist during Row 15!
04: // In 16-bit Control: reg [12:0] count; reg completed; // Holds at count == 13'h100F (cycle 4111)!
05: // In 8-bit Comparator:  if (CompStart == 0) BestDist <= 8'hFF;   // Ties when newDist == 8'hFF!
06: // In 16-bit Comparator: if (CompStart == 0) BestDist <= 16'hFFFF; // 16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF is always TRUE!
// --- Course Project Syllabus Requirements Checklist (Items 1-5) ---
07: // [x] Clock Period = 1.923 ns (520.02 MHz) | Input Delay = 0.5 ns | Output Delay = 0.5 ns | Uncertainty = 0.2 ns
08: // [x] Exclude Reference (RMEM 256x8) and Search (SMEM 1024x8) memories from top.v synthesis!
TERM_SFSU: [926784856@mahmoodi me_asic_new_v1]$ grep -E 'BestDist|motionX|motionY|PASS' logs/*.log | tail -n 4
OUT_OK:    All SAD D(i,j), motion vector (i-8, j-8), and cycle-4111 hold equations verified in VCS!
# --- Additional Live Diagnostic & Rubric Verification Commands for This Step ---

cmd_explanations: - **`Reference Macroblock`** → **`R = r_{m,n}, m,n in [0,15]`**: 256 x 8-bit ROM_R | Current 16x16 pixel block being encoded
- **`Search Window`** → **`S = s_{x,y}, x,y in [0,30]`**: 1024 x 8-bit ROM_S | 31x31 region in previous frame (+/-8 pixels)

- **`Distortion Metric`** → **`D(i, j)`**: 8-bit (orig) / 16-bit | Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) over 256 pixels

foundation_text: Chapter 10 Sec. 10.4 Foundation Bridge (Page 13): Each grayscale video pixel is an 8-bit unsigned integer `0..255` (`2^8 = 256` levels). Comparing a 16x16 Reference macroblock (`256` pixels) against a 16x16 Search candidate adds 256 absolute differences `|R - S|`. Since each pixel difference can be up to `255`, the maximum possible sum is `256 * 255 = 65,280` (`16'hFF00`).

three_methods.method1: Behavior on Page 13 (Page 13: Block-Matching Motion Estimation Concept (Chapter 10, Section 10.4, pp. 143-145)): Trace how the 16 Processing Elements (`PE0..PE15`) evaluate 16 horizontal candidates `u in [-8..+7]` in parallel while `R` shifts through `Rpipe[0..14]`.
three_methods.method2: Mathematical & Bit-Width Proof: `SAD(u,v) = sum_{i=0..15} sum_{j=0..15} |R(i,j) - S(i+u, j+v)|`. Bit width required = `ceil(log2(256 * 255 + 1)) = 16 bits` (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`). An 8-bit register (`max 255 = 8'hFF`) overflows on Row 0 whenever average `|R-S| >= 1`!
three_methods.method3: RTL & Hardware Mapping: Each PE needs an 8-bit 2:1 mux (`S1` vs `S2`), an 8-bit absolute difference circuit (`|R - S|`), a 16-bit adder, and a 16-bit DFF accumulator (`Accumulate[15:0]`), feeding a 16:1 mux and 16-bit comparator (`BestDist[15:0]`).

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Ch. 10 SAD Bit-Width & Saturation Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 13 · Bit-Width & Saturation Math (Midterm Q2 Connection)] What is the maximum possible SAD value for a 16x16 macroblock of 8-bit pixels (`0..255`), and how many bits are required to represent it without saturation or wrap-around?
options: A) Max SAD = 255 (8'hFF); requires 8 bits.
B) Max SAD = 4,080 (16'h0FF0); requires 12 bits.
C) Max SAD = 65,280 (16'hFF00 = 256 pixels * 255 max diff); requires 16 bits (with 16'hFFFF = 65,535 reserved as the initial BestDist).
D) Max SAD = 65,536; requires 17 bits.
quiz_questions.hint: Multiply the total number of pixels in a 16x16 macroblock (`16 * 16 = 256`) by the maximum possible 8-bit pixel difference (`|255 - 0| = 255`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `255 (8'hFF)` is the maximum difference of a SINGLE pixel, not the sum across 256 pixels!
Incorrect — `4,080 (16 * 255)` is the maximum SAD of a single 16-pixel row (`Row 0`), not all 16 rows (`256` pixels).
Correct! `256 pixels * 255 max diff = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`) prevents overflow and leaves `16'hFFFF` as a valid sentinel initial value for `BestDist`!
Incorrect — `65,280` fits comfortably inside 16 unsigned bits (`0..65,535`), so a 17th bit is unnecessary.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: C) `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, each with max difference `|0 - 255| = 255`. Thus `SAD_max = 256 * 255 = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. three_methods.method1: Behavior on Page 14 (Page 14: Sum of Absolute Differences (SAD) Distortion Equation D(i,j)  -  Hand Calculation): Trace how the 16 Processing Elements (`PE0..PE15`) evaluate 16 horizontal candidates `u in [-8..+7]` in parallel while `R` shifts through `Rpipe[0..14]`.

quiz_questions.q: [Page 15 · Bit-Width & Saturation Math (Midterm Q2 Connection)] What is the maximum possible SAD value for a 16x16 macroblock of 8-bit pixels (`0..255`), and how many bits are required to represent it without saturation or wrap-around?
options: A) Max SAD = 255 (8'hFF); requires 8 bits.
B) Max SAD = 4,080 (16'h0FF0); requires 12 bits.
C) Max SAD = 65,280 (16'hFF00 = 256 pixels * 255 max diff); requires 16 bits (with 16'hFFFF = 65,535 reserved as the initial BestDist).
D) Max SAD = 65,536; requires 17 bits.
quiz_questions.hint: Multiply the total number of pixels in a 16x16 macroblock (`16 * 16 = 256`) by the maximum possible 8-bit pixel difference (`|255 - 0| = 255`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `255 (8'hFF)` is the maximum difference of a SINGLE pixel, not the sum across 256 pixels!
Incorrect — `4,080 (16 * 255)` is the maximum SAD of a single 16-pixel row (`Row 0`), not all 16 rows (`256` pixels).
Correct! `256 pixels * 255 max diff = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`) prevents overflow and leaves `16'hFFFF` as a valid sentinel initial value for `BestDist`!
Incorrect — `65,280` fits comfortably inside 16 unsigned bits (`0..65,535`), so a 17th bit is unnecessary.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: C) `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, each with max difference `|0 - 255| = 255`. Thus `SAD_max = 256 * 255 = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits allows `BestDist` to initialize to `16'hFFFF (65,535)` so even a max-contrast block (`16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF`) triggers `newBest = 1`!

Incorrect — `8'h08` and `8'h05` are positive `+8` and `+5`, while `8'hF7` is `-9`.

trap_notes: GREEN:Why Dual Search Ports (S1 and S2) Are Needed:
When PE0 begins row m+1 of candidate (0,j) at horizontal offset 0, PE1..PE15 are still finishing row m
at horizontal offsets 16..30! S1 supplies the left half of the search row while S2 supplies the right half.
code_block: // Inside module PE: 2-to-1 MUX selects between broadcast search buses S1 and S2:

foundation_text: Chapter 10 Sec. 10.4 Foundation Bridge (Page 16): Each grayscale video pixel is an 8-bit unsigned integer `0..255` (`2^8 = 256` levels). Comparing a 16x16 Reference macroblock (`256` pixels) against a 16x16 Search candidate adds 256 absolute differences `|R - S|`. Since each pixel difference can be up to `255`, the maximum possible sum is `256 * 255 = 65,280` (`16'hFF00`).

three_methods.method1: Behavior on Page 16 (Page 16: 16-PE 1D Systolic Array Architecture & Dual Search Memory Ports (S1, S2)): Trace how the 16 Processing Elements (`PE0..PE15`) evaluate 16 horizontal candidates `u in [-8..+7]` in parallel while `R` shifts through `Rpipe[0..14]`.
three_methods.method2: Mathematical & Bit-Width Proof: `SAD(u,v) = sum_{i=0..15} sum_{j=0..15} |R(i,j) - S(i+u, j+v)|`. Bit width required = `ceil(log2(256 * 255 + 1)) = 16 bits` (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`). An 8-bit register (`max 255 = 8'hFF`) overflows on Row 0 whenever average `|R-S| >= 1`!
three_methods.method3: RTL & Hardware Mapping: Each PE needs an 8-bit 2:1 mux (`S1` vs `S2`), an 8-bit absolute difference circuit (`|R - S|`), a 16-bit adder, and a 16-bit DFF accumulator (`Accumulate[15:0]`), feeding a 16:1 mux and 16-bit comparator (`BestDist[15:0]`).

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Ch. 10 SAD Bit-Width & Saturation Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 16 · Bit-Width & Saturation Math (Midterm Q2 Connection)] What is the maximum possible SAD value for a 16x16 macroblock of 8-bit pixels (`0..255`), and how many bits are required to represent it without saturation or wrap-around?
options: A) Max SAD = 255 (8'hFF); requires 8 bits.
B) Max SAD = 4,080 (16'h0FF0); requires 12 bits.
C) Max SAD = 65,280 (16'hFF00 = 256 pixels * 255 max diff); requires 16 bits (with 16'hFFFF = 65,535 reserved as the initial BestDist).
D) Max SAD = 65,536; requires 17 bits.
quiz_questions.hint: Multiply the total number of pixels in a 16x16 macroblock (`16 * 16 = 256`) by the maximum possible 8-bit pixel difference (`|255 - 0| = 255`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `255 (8'hFF)` is the maximum difference of a SINGLE pixel, not the sum across 256 pixels!
Incorrect — `4,080 (16 * 255)` is the maximum SAD of a single 16-pixel row (`Row 0`), not all 16 rows (`256` pixels).
Correct! `256 pixels * 255 max diff = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`) prevents overflow and leaves `16'hFFFF` as a valid sentinel initial value for `BestDist`!
Incorrect — `65,280` fits comfortably inside 16 unsigned bits (`0..65,535`), so a 17th bit is unnecessary.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: C) `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, each with max difference `|0 - 255| = 255`. Thus `SAD_max = 256 * 255 = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits allows `BestDist` to initialize to `16'hFFFF (65,535)` so even a max-contrast block (`16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF`) triggers `newBest = 1`!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Two's-Complement Motion Vectors & Systolic Addressing)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 16 · Two's-Complement Motion Vectors] In our `[-8, +7]` search range, what are the 8-bit two's-complement hexadecimal values for `motionX = -8`, `motionX = -5`, and `motionY = +7`?
quiz_questions.hint: For a negative integer `-k` in 8-bit two's complement, compute `256 - k` and convert to hexadecimal (`256 - 8 = 248`, `256 - 5 = 251`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `8'h88` and `8'h85` are sign-magnitude encodings, whereas Verilog arithmetic uses two's complement.
Incorrect — `8'h08` and `8'h05` are positive `+8` and `+5`, while `8'hF7` is `-9`.
Incorrect — `8'hFF` is `-1` and `8'hFA` is `-6`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In 8-bit two's complement (`256 + negative_offset`): `-8 -> 256 - 8 = 248 = 8'hF8`; `-5 -> 256 - 5 = 251 = 8'hFB`; `+7 -> 8'h07`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Systolic Pipeline Latency & Throughput Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 16 · Advanced Systolic Array Timing] Why does a full 256-candidate macroblock search across the 16-PE systolic array take exactly `4,111` clock cycles (`count == 13'h100F`), and what is the throughput in macroblocks/second at `520 MHz`?
options: A) 256 candidates * 256 pixels = 65,536 cycles (7,934 macroblocks/sec)

B) 16 vertical search rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles + 15 Rpipe pipeline fill cycles for PE15 = 4,111 cycles (`7.906 us` per macroblock = `126,489 macroblocks/sec`, or `30.9 frames/sec` for 1024x1024 video!)
C) 16 PEs * 16 rows = 256 cycles
D) 4,095 cycles (`12'hFFF`)
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that all 16 horizontal candidates in a row are computed in parallel across `PE0..PE15` in 256 cycles, but `PE15` receives `R` delayed by 15 `Rpipe` stages!
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `65,536` cycles would be a sequential 1-PE engine; our 16-PE systolic array achieves a 16x speedup!

Correct! `16 rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles`, plus `15` cycles for `Rpipe[0..14]` to reach `PE15` = `4,111 cycles` (`13'h100F`). At `1.923 ns/cycle`, `4,111 * 1.923 ns = 7.906 us` (`126,489 macroblocks/s`).
Incorrect — Each candidate requires accumulating `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, not 16 pixels.
Incorrect — At cycle `4,095`, `PE15` still has 15 pixels left in the `Rpipe` shift register before completing its 256-pixel sum at cycle `4,111`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `4,096 + 15 = 4,111` clock cycles (`13'h100F`). Dividing `520,000,000 Hz / 4,111 cycles = 126,489.9 macroblocks/sec`, which processes `4,096` macroblocks (a full `1024x1024` frame) at `30.88 fps`!

foundation_text: Chapter 10 Sec. 10.4 Foundation Bridge (Page 17): Each grayscale video pixel is an 8-bit unsigned integer `0..255` (`2^8 = 256` levels). Comparing a 16x16 Reference macroblock (`256` pixels) against a 16x16 Search candidate adds 256 absolute differences `|R - S|`. Since each pixel difference can be up to `255`, the maximum possible sum is `256 * 255 = 65,280` (`16'hFF00`).

three_methods.method1: Behavior on Page 17 (Page 17: Understanding the 15-Cycle Rpipe Shift Register Pipeline Fill): Trace how the 16 Processing Elements (`PE0..PE15`) evaluate 16 horizontal candidates `u in [-8..+7]` in parallel while `R` shifts through `Rpipe[0..14]`.
three_methods.method2: Mathematical & Bit-Width Proof: `SAD(u,v) = sum_{i=0..15} sum_{j=0..15} |R(i,j) - S(i+u, j+v)|`. Bit width required = `ceil(log2(256 * 255 + 1)) = 16 bits` (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`). An 8-bit register (`max 255 = 8'hFF`) overflows on Row 0 whenever average `|R-S| >= 1`!
three_methods.method3: RTL & Hardware Mapping: Each PE needs an 8-bit 2:1 mux (`S1` vs `S2`), an 8-bit absolute difference circuit (`|R - S|`), a 16-bit adder, and a 16-bit DFF accumulator (`Accumulate[15:0]`), feeding a 16:1 mux and 16-bit comparator (`BestDist[15:0]`).

choice_diagnostics: Correct! `snap_step "page017_understanding_15_cycle_rpipe" 'python3 -c` performs: Loads the telemetry bridge and wraps the page's command sequence in the Expected-Outcome Verifier. And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Ch. 10 SAD Bit-Width & Saturation Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 17 · Bit-Width & Saturation Math (Midterm Q2 Connection)] What is the maximum possible SAD value for a 16x16 macroblock of 8-bit pixels (`0..255`), and how many bits are required to represent it without saturation or wrap-around?
options: A) Max SAD = 255 (8'hFF); requires 8 bits.
B) Max SAD = 4,080 (16'h0FF0); requires 12 bits.
C) Max SAD = 65,280 (16'hFF00 = 256 pixels * 255 max diff); requires 16 bits (with 16'hFFFF = 65,535 reserved as the initial BestDist).
D) Max SAD = 65,536; requires 17 bits.
quiz_questions.hint: Multiply the total number of pixels in a 16x16 macroblock (`16 * 16 = 256`) by the maximum possible 8-bit pixel difference (`|255 - 0| = 255`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `255 (8'hFF)` is the maximum difference of a SINGLE pixel, not the sum across 256 pixels!
Incorrect — `4,080 (16 * 255)` is the maximum SAD of a single 16-pixel row (`Row 0`), not all 16 rows (`256` pixels).
Correct! `256 pixels * 255 max diff = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`) prevents overflow and leaves `16'hFFFF` as a valid sentinel initial value for `BestDist`!
Incorrect — `65,280` fits comfortably inside 16 unsigned bits (`0..65,535`), so a 17th bit is unnecessary.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: C) `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, each with max difference `|0 - 255| = 255`. Thus `SAD_max = 256 * 255 = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits allows `BestDist` to initialize to `16'hFFFF (65,535)` so even a max-contrast block (`16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF`) triggers `newBest = 1`!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Two's-Complement Motion Vectors & Systolic Addressing)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 17 · Two's-Complement Motion Vectors] In our `[-8, +7]` search range, what are the 8-bit two's-complement hexadecimal values for `motionX = -8`, `motionX = -5`, and `motionY = +7`?
quiz_questions.hint: For a negative integer `-k` in 8-bit two's complement, compute `256 - k` and convert to hexadecimal (`256 - 8 = 248`, `256 - 5 = 251`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `8'h88` and `8'h85` are sign-magnitude encodings, whereas Verilog arithmetic uses two's complement.
Incorrect — `8'h08` and `8'h05` are positive `+8` and `+5`, while `8'hF7` is `-9`.
Incorrect — `8'hFF` is `-1` and `8'hFA` is `-6`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In 8-bit two's complement (`256 + negative_offset`): `-8 -> 256 - 8 = 248 = 8'hF8`; `-5 -> 256 - 5 = 251 = 8'hFB`; `+7 -> 8'h07`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Systolic Pipeline Latency & Throughput Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 17 · Advanced Systolic Array Timing] Why does a full 256-candidate macroblock search across the 16-PE systolic array take exactly `4,111` clock cycles (`count == 13'h100F`), and what is the throughput in macroblocks/second at `520 MHz`?
options: A) 256 candidates * 256 pixels = 65,536 cycles (7,934 macroblocks/sec)

B) 16 vertical search rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles + 15 Rpipe pipeline fill cycles for PE15 = 4,111 cycles (`7.906 us` per macroblock = `126,489 macroblocks/sec`, or `30.9 frames/sec` for 1024x1024 video!)
C) 16 PEs * 16 rows = 256 cycles
D) 4,095 cycles (`12'hFFF`)
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that all 16 horizontal candidates in a row are computed in parallel across `PE0..PE15` in 256 cycles, but `PE15` receives `R` delayed by 15 `Rpipe` stages!
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `65,536` cycles would be a sequential 1-PE engine; our 16-PE systolic array achieves a 16x speedup!

Correct! `16 rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles`, plus `15` cycles for `Rpipe[0..14]` to reach `PE15` = `4,111 cycles` (`13'h100F`). At `1.923 ns/cycle`, `4,111 * 1.923 ns = 7.906 us` (`126,489 macroblocks/s`).
Incorrect — Each candidate requires accumulating `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, not 16 pixels.
Incorrect — At cycle `4,095`, `PE15` still has 15 pixels left in the `Rpipe` shift register before completing its 256-pixel sum at cycle `4,111`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `4,096 + 15 = 4,111` clock cycles (`13'h100F`). Dividing `520,000,000 Hz / 4,111 cycles = 126,489.9 macroblocks/sec`, which processes `4,096` macroblocks (a full `1024x1024` frame) at `30.88 fps`!

foundation_text: Chapter 10 Sec. 10.4 Foundation Bridge (Page 18): Each grayscale video pixel is an 8-bit unsigned integer `0..255` (`2^8 = 256` levels). Comparing a 16x16 Reference macroblock (`256` pixels) against a 16x16 Search candidate adds 256 absolute differences `|R - S|`. Since each pixel difference can be up to `255`, the maximum possible sum is `256 * 255 = 65,280` (`16'hFF00`).

three_methods.method1: Behavior on Page 18 (Page 18: Reproducing Lecture Notes Table 10.1 (p. 146)  -  Complete 4,111-Cycle Schedule): Trace how the 16 Processing Elements (`PE0..PE15`) evaluate 16 horizontal candidates `u in [-8..+7]` in parallel while `R` shifts through `Rpipe[0..14]`.
three_methods.method2: Mathematical & Bit-Width Proof: `SAD(u,v) = sum_{i=0..15} sum_{j=0..15} |R(i,j) - S(i+u, j+v)|`. Bit width required = `ceil(log2(256 * 255 + 1)) = 16 bits` (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`). An 8-bit register (`max 255 = 8'hFF`) overflows on Row 0 whenever average `|R-S| >= 1`!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Ch. 10 SAD Bit-Width & Saturation Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 18 · Bit-Width & Saturation Math (Midterm Q2 Connection)] What is the maximum possible SAD value for a 16x16 macroblock of 8-bit pixels (`0..255`), and how many bits are required to represent it without saturation or wrap-around?
options: A) Max SAD = 255 (8'hFF); requires 8 bits.
B) Max SAD = 4,080 (16'h0FF0); requires 12 bits.
C) Max SAD = 65,280 (16'hFF00 = 256 pixels * 255 max diff); requires 16 bits (with 16'hFFFF = 65,535 reserved as the initial BestDist).
D) Max SAD = 65,536; requires 17 bits.
quiz_questions.hint: Multiply the total number of pixels in a 16x16 macroblock (`16 * 16 = 256`) by the maximum possible 8-bit pixel difference (`|255 - 0| = 255`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `255 (8'hFF)` is the maximum difference of a SINGLE pixel, not the sum across 256 pixels!
Incorrect — `4,080 (16 * 255)` is the maximum SAD of a single 16-pixel row (`Row 0`), not all 16 rows (`256` pixels).
Correct! `256 pixels * 255 max diff = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`) prevents overflow and leaves `16'hFFFF` as a valid sentinel initial value for `BestDist`!
Incorrect — `65,280` fits comfortably inside 16 unsigned bits (`0..65,535`), so a 17th bit is unnecessary.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: C) `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, each with max difference `|0 - 255| = 255`. Thus `SAD_max = 256 * 255 = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits allows `BestDist` to initialize to `16'hFFFF (65,535)` so even a max-contrast block (`16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF`) triggers `newBest = 1`!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Two's-Complement Motion Vectors & Systolic Addressing)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 18 · Two's-Complement Motion Vectors] In our `[-8, +7]` search range, what are the 8-bit two's-complement hexadecimal values for `motionX = -8`, `motionX = -5`, and `motionY = +7`?
quiz_questions.hint: For a negative integer `-k` in 8-bit two's complement, compute `256 - k` and convert to hexadecimal (`256 - 8 = 248`, `256 - 5 = 251`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `8'h88` and `8'h85` are sign-magnitude encodings, whereas Verilog arithmetic uses two's complement.
Incorrect — `8'h08` and `8'h05` are positive `+8` and `+5`, while `8'hF7` is `-9`.
Incorrect — `8'hFF` is `-1` and `8'hFA` is `-6`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In 8-bit two's complement (`256 + negative_offset`): `-8 -> 256 - 8 = 248 = 8'hF8`; `-5 -> 256 - 5 = 251 = 8'hFB`; `+7 -> 8'h07`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Systolic Pipeline Latency & Throughput Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 18 · Advanced Systolic Array Timing] Why does a full 256-candidate macroblock search across the 16-PE systolic array take exactly `4,111` clock cycles (`count == 13'h100F`), and what is the throughput in macroblocks/second at `520 MHz`?
options: A) 256 candidates * 256 pixels = 65,536 cycles (7,934 macroblocks/sec)

B) 16 vertical search rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles + 15 Rpipe pipeline fill cycles for PE15 = 4,111 cycles (`7.906 us` per macroblock = `126,489 macroblocks/sec`, or `30.9 frames/sec` for 1024x1024 video!)
C) 16 PEs * 16 rows = 256 cycles
D) 4,095 cycles (`12'hFFF`)
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that all 16 horizontal candidates in a row are computed in parallel across `PE0..PE15` in 256 cycles, but `PE15` receives `R` delayed by 15 `Rpipe` stages!
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `65,536` cycles would be a sequential 1-PE engine; our 16-PE systolic array achieves a 16x speedup!

Correct! `16 rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles`, plus `15` cycles for `Rpipe[0..14]` to reach `PE15` = `4,111 cycles` (`13'h100F`). At `1.923 ns/cycle`, `4,111 * 1.923 ns = 7.906 us` (`126,489 macroblocks/s`).
Incorrect — Each candidate requires accumulating `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, not 16 pixels.
Incorrect — At cycle `4,095`, `PE15` still has 15 pixels left in the `Rpipe` shift register before completing its 256-pixel sum at cycle `4,111`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `4,096 + 15 = 4,111` clock cycles (`13'h100F`). Dividing `520,000,000 Hz / 4,111 cycles = 126,489.9 macroblocks/sec`, which processes `4,096` macroblocks (a full `1024x1024` frame) at `30.88 fps`!

trap_notes: GREEN:Clever Hardware Trick: Multiplying by 31 Without a Multiplier!
Since the search window is 31 pixels wide, row (j+m) starts at byte address 31*(j+m).
In binary, 31 * temp = (32 - 1) * temp = {temp[4:0], 5'b00000} - temp! Zero multipliers needed!
code_block: // In module Control (Lecture Notes p. 149): Multiplying row index by 31 using shift-and-subtract:
AddressR = count[7:0];                                      // Reference pixel address (0..255)
temp = count[11:8] + count[7:4];                            // Search row index y = j + m (0..30)
AddressS1 = ({temp[4:0], 5'b00000} - temp) + count[3:0];    // 31*y + n (left half cols 0..15)
temp = temp - 1;                                            // Previous search row y - 1
AddressS2 = ({temp[4:0], 5'b00000} - temp) + count[3:0] + 16; // 31*(y-1) + n + 16 (right half cols 16..30)

foundation_text: Chapter 10 Sec. 10.4 Foundation Bridge (Page 19): Each grayscale video pixel is an 8-bit unsigned integer `0..255` (`2^8 = 256` levels). Comparing a 16x16 Reference macroblock (`256` pixels) against a 16x16 Search candidate adds 256 absolute differences `|R - S|`. Since each pixel difference can be up to `255`, the maximum possible sum is `256 * 255 = 65,280` (`16'hFF00`).

three_methods.method2: Mathematical & Bit-Width Proof: `SAD(u,v) = sum_{i=0..15} sum_{j=0..15} |R(i,j) - S(i+u, j+v)|`. Bit width required = `ceil(log2(256 * 255 + 1)) = 16 bits` (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`). An 8-bit register (`max 255 = 8'hFF`) overflows on Row 0 whenever average `|R-S| >= 1`!

And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Ch. 10 SAD Bit-Width & Saturation Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 19 · Bit-Width & Saturation Math (Midterm Q2 Connection)] What is the maximum possible SAD value for a 16x16 macroblock of 8-bit pixels (`0..255`), and how many bits are required to represent it without saturation or wrap-around?
options: A) Max SAD = 255 (8'hFF); requires 8 bits.
B) Max SAD = 4,080 (16'h0FF0); requires 12 bits.
C) Max SAD = 65,280 (16'hFF00 = 256 pixels * 255 max diff); requires 16 bits (with 16'hFFFF = 65,535 reserved as the initial BestDist).
D) Max SAD = 65,536; requires 17 bits.
quiz_questions.hint: Multiply the total number of pixels in a 16x16 macroblock (`16 * 16 = 256`) by the maximum possible 8-bit pixel difference (`|255 - 0| = 255`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `255 (8'hFF)` is the maximum difference of a SINGLE pixel, not the sum across 256 pixels!
Incorrect — `4,080 (16 * 255)` is the maximum SAD of a single 16-pixel row (`Row 0`), not all 16 rows (`256` pixels).
Correct! `256 pixels * 255 max diff = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`) prevents overflow and leaves `16'hFFFF` as a valid sentinel initial value for `BestDist`!
Incorrect — `65,280` fits comfortably inside 16 unsigned bits (`0..65,535`), so a 17th bit is unnecessary.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: C) `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, each with max difference `|0 - 255| = 255`. Thus `SAD_max = 256 * 255 = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits allows `BestDist` to initialize to `16'hFFFF (65,535)` so even a max-contrast block (`16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF`) triggers `newBest = 1`!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Two's-Complement Motion Vectors & Systolic Addressing)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 19 · Two's-Complement Motion Vectors] In our `[-8, +7]` search range, what are the 8-bit two's-complement hexadecimal values for `motionX = -8`, `motionX = -5`, and `motionY = +7`?
quiz_questions.hint: For a negative integer `-k` in 8-bit two's complement, compute `256 - k` and convert to hexadecimal (`256 - 8 = 248`, `256 - 5 = 251`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `8'h88` and `8'h85` are sign-magnitude encodings, whereas Verilog arithmetic uses two's complement.
Incorrect — `8'h08` and `8'h05` are positive `+8` and `+5`, while `8'hF7` is `-9`.
Incorrect — `8'hFF` is `-1` and `8'hFA` is `-6`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In 8-bit two's complement (`256 + negative_offset`): `-8 -> 256 - 8 = 248 = 8'hF8`; `-5 -> 256 - 5 = 251 = 8'hFB`; `+7 -> 8'h07`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Systolic Pipeline Latency & Throughput Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 19 · Advanced Systolic Array Timing] Why does a full 256-candidate macroblock search across the 16-PE systolic array take exactly `4,111` clock cycles (`count == 13'h100F`), and what is the throughput in macroblocks/second at `520 MHz`?
options: A) 256 candidates * 256 pixels = 65,536 cycles (7,934 macroblocks/sec)

B) 16 vertical search rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles + 15 Rpipe pipeline fill cycles for PE15 = 4,111 cycles (`7.906 us` per macroblock = `126,489 macroblocks/sec`, or `30.9 frames/sec` for 1024x1024 video!)
C) 16 PEs * 16 rows = 256 cycles
D) 4,095 cycles (`12'hFFF`)
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that all 16 horizontal candidates in a row are computed in parallel across `PE0..PE15` in 256 cycles, but `PE15` receives `R` delayed by 15 `Rpipe` stages!
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `65,536` cycles would be a sequential 1-PE engine; our 16-PE systolic array achieves a 16x speedup!

Correct! `16 rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles`, plus `15` cycles for `Rpipe[0..14]` to reach `PE15` = `4,111 cycles` (`13'h100F`). At `1.923 ns/cycle`, `4,111 * 1.923 ns = 7.906 us` (`126,489 macroblocks/s`).
Incorrect — Each candidate requires accumulating `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, not 16 pixels.
Incorrect — At cycle `4,095`, `PE15` still has 15 pixels left in the `Rpipe` shift register before completing its 256-pixel sum at cycle `4,111`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `4,096 + 15 = 4,111` clock cycles (`13'h100F`). Dividing `520,000,000 Hz / 4,111 cycles = 126,489.9 macroblocks/sec`, which processes `4,096` macroblocks (a full `1024x1024` frame) at `30.88 fps`!

title: Page 20: Deep Dive into the 8-Bit Saturating Adder in PE (Section 10.4.1, p. 147)
subtitle: Why Professor Mahmoodi's Baseline PE Uses {Carry, AccumulateIn} Saturation at 8'hFF

v_desc: Ch. 10 Sec. 10.4 SAD Math, 8-Bit Saturation Trap & 16-Bit Theory
trap_notes: BLUE:Why Chapter 10 Included Saturation in the 8-Bit Design (p. 147):
If an 8-bit accumulator wrapped modulo 256, a terrible block with D(i,j) = 256 would wrap to 8'h00 and look
like a perfect zero-distortion match! Saturation clamps any sum >= 255 at 8'hFF to prevent modulo wrap-around.
code_block: // Original 8-bit saturating accumulator in module PE (Lecture Notes p. 147):
{Carry, AccumulateIn} = Accumulate + difference; // 9-bit addition captures Carry out of bit 7
if (Carry == 1) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;            // Clamp at 255 (8'hFF) if unsigned overflow occurs
if (newDist == 1) AccumulateIn = difference;     // Reset accumulator to 1st pixel diff on new block
// --- Interactive Hardware Verification of This Architectural Step on mahmoodi ---

// --- Comparing 8-Bit Baseline (rtl/8bit/top.v) vs. 16-Bit Non-Saturating Upgrade (rtl/16bit/top.v) ---
01: // In 8-bit PE:  {Carry, AccumulateIn} = Accumulate + difference; if (Carry == 1) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;
02: // In 16-bit PE: AccumulateIn = Accumulate + {8'd0, difference};  // Exact sum up to 256*255 = 65,280 (16'hFF00)
03: // In 8-bit Control:  reg [11:0] count; // Wraps to 0 at cycle 4096 -> resets BestDist during Row 15!
04: // In 16-bit Control: reg [12:0] count; reg completed; // Holds at count == 13'h100F (cycle 4111)!
05: // In 8-bit Comparator:  if (CompStart == 0) BestDist <= 8'hFF;   // Ties when newDist == 8'hFF!
06: // In 16-bit Comparator: if (CompStart == 0) BestDist <= 16'hFFFF; // 16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF is always TRUE!

foundation_text: Chapter 10 Sec. 10.4 Foundation Bridge (Page 20): Each grayscale video pixel is an 8-bit unsigned integer `0..255` (`2^8 = 256` levels). Comparing a 16x16 Reference macroblock (`256` pixels) against a 16x16 Search candidate adds 256 absolute differences `|R - S|`. Since each pixel difference can be up to `255`, the maximum possible sum is `256 * 255 = 65,280` (`16'hFF00`).

three_methods.method1: Behavior on Page 20 (Page 20: Deep Dive into the 8-Bit Saturating Adder in PE (Section 10.4.1, p. 147)): Trace how the 16 Processing Elements (`PE0..PE15`) evaluate 16 horizontal candidates `u in [-8..+7]` in parallel while `R` shifts through `Rpipe[0..14]`.
three_methods.method2: Mathematical & Bit-Width Proof: `SAD(u,v) = sum_{i=0..15} sum_{j=0..15} |R(i,j) - S(i+u, j+v)|`. Bit width required = `ceil(log2(256 * 255 + 1)) = 16 bits` (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`). An 8-bit register (`max 255 = 8'hFF`) overflows on Row 0 whenever average `|R-S| >= 1`!
three_methods.method3: RTL & Hardware Mapping: Each PE needs an 8-bit 2:1 mux (`S1` vs `S2`), an 8-bit absolute difference circuit (`|R - S|`), a 16-bit adder, and a 16-bit DFF accumulator (`Accumulate[15:0]`), feeding a 16:1 mux and 16-bit comparator (`BestDist[15:0]`).

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Ch. 10 SAD Bit-Width & Saturation Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 20 · Bit-Width & Saturation Math (Midterm Q2 Connection)] What is the maximum possible SAD value for a 16x16 macroblock of 8-bit pixels (`0..255`), and how many bits are required to represent it without saturation or wrap-around?
options: A) Max SAD = 255 (8'hFF); requires 8 bits.
B) Max SAD = 4,080 (16'h0FF0); requires 12 bits.
C) Max SAD = 65,280 (16'hFF00 = 256 pixels * 255 max diff); requires 16 bits (with 16'hFFFF = 65,535 reserved as the initial BestDist).
D) Max SAD = 65,536; requires 17 bits.
quiz_questions.hint: Multiply the total number of pixels in a 16x16 macroblock (`16 * 16 = 256`) by the maximum possible 8-bit pixel difference (`|255 - 0| = 255`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `255 (8'hFF)` is the maximum difference of a SINGLE pixel, not the sum across 256 pixels!
Incorrect — `4,080 (16 * 255)` is the maximum SAD of a single 16-pixel row (`Row 0`), not all 16 rows (`256` pixels).
Correct! `256 pixels * 255 max diff = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`) prevents overflow and leaves `16'hFFFF` as a valid sentinel initial value for `BestDist`!
Incorrect — `65,280` fits comfortably inside 16 unsigned bits (`0..65,535`), so a 17th bit is unnecessary.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: C) `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, each with max difference `|0 - 255| = 255`. Thus `SAD_max = 256 * 255 = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits allows `BestDist` to initialize to `16'hFFFF (65,535)` so even a max-contrast block (`16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF`) triggers `newBest = 1`!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Two's-Complement Motion Vectors & Systolic Addressing)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 20 · Two's-Complement Motion Vectors] In our `[-8, +7]` search range, what are the 8-bit two's-complement hexadecimal values for `motionX = -8`, `motionX = -5`, and `motionY = +7`?
quiz_questions.hint: For a negative integer `-k` in 8-bit two's complement, compute `256 - k` and convert to hexadecimal (`256 - 8 = 248`, `256 - 5 = 251`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `8'h88` and `8'h85` are sign-magnitude encodings, whereas Verilog arithmetic uses two's complement.
Incorrect — `8'h08` and `8'h05` are positive `+8` and `+5`, while `8'hF7` is `-9`.
Incorrect — `8'hFF` is `-1` and `8'hFA` is `-6`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In 8-bit two's complement (`256 + negative_offset`): `-8 -> 256 - 8 = 248 = 8'hF8`; `-5 -> 256 - 5 = 251 = 8'hFB`; `+7 -> 8'h07`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Systolic Pipeline Latency & Throughput Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 20 · Advanced Systolic Array Timing] Why does a full 256-candidate macroblock search across the 16-PE systolic array take exactly `4,111` clock cycles (`count == 13'h100F`), and what is the throughput in macroblocks/second at `520 MHz`?
options: A) 256 candidates * 256 pixels = 65,536 cycles (7,934 macroblocks/sec)

B) 16 vertical search rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles + 15 Rpipe pipeline fill cycles for PE15 = 4,111 cycles (`7.906 us` per macroblock = `126,489 macroblocks/sec`, or `30.9 frames/sec` for 1024x1024 video!)
C) 16 PEs * 16 rows = 256 cycles
D) 4,095 cycles (`12'hFFF`)
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that all 16 horizontal candidates in a row are computed in parallel across `PE0..PE15` in 256 cycles, but `PE15` receives `R` delayed by 15 `Rpipe` stages!
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `65,536` cycles would be a sequential 1-PE engine; our 16-PE systolic array achieves a 16x speedup!

Correct! `16 rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles`, plus `15` cycles for `Rpipe[0..14]` to reach `PE15` = `4,111 cycles` (`13'h100F`). At `1.923 ns/cycle`, `4,111 * 1.923 ns = 7.906 us` (`126,489 macroblocks/s`).
Incorrect — Each candidate requires accumulating `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, not 16 pixels.
Incorrect — At cycle `4,095`, `PE15` still has 15 pixels left in the `Rpipe` shift register before completing its 256-pixel sum at cycle `4,111`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `4,096 + 15 = 4,111` clock cycles (`13'h100F`). Dividing `520,000,000 Hz / 4,111 cycles = 126,489.9 macroblocks/sec`, which processes `4,096` macroblocks (a full `1024x1024` frame) at `30.88 fps`!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Ch. 10 SAD Bit-Width & Saturation Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 21 · Bit-Width & Saturation Math (Midterm Q2 Connection)] What is the maximum possible SAD value for a 16x16 macroblock of 8-bit pixels (`0..255`), and how many bits are required to represent it without saturation or wrap-around?
options: A) Max SAD = 255 (8'hFF); requires 8 bits.
B) Max SAD = 4,080 (16'h0FF0); requires 12 bits.
C) Max SAD = 65,280 (16'hFF00 = 256 pixels * 255 max diff); requires 16 bits (with 16'hFFFF = 65,535 reserved as the initial BestDist).
D) Max SAD = 65,536; requires 17 bits.
quiz_questions.hint: Multiply the total number of pixels in a 16x16 macroblock (`16 * 16 = 256`) by the maximum possible 8-bit pixel difference (`|255 - 0| = 255`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `255 (8'hFF)` is the maximum difference of a SINGLE pixel, not the sum across 256 pixels!
Incorrect — `4,080 (16 * 255)` is the maximum SAD of a single 16-pixel row (`Row 0`), not all 16 rows (`256` pixels).
Correct! `256 pixels * 255 max diff = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`) prevents overflow and leaves `16'hFFFF` as a valid sentinel initial value for `BestDist`!
Incorrect — `65,280` fits comfortably inside 16 unsigned bits (`0..65,535`), so a 17th bit is unnecessary.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: C) `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, each with max difference `|0 - 255| = 255`. Thus `SAD_max = 256 * 255 = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits allows `BestDist` to initialize to `16'hFFFF (65,535)` so even a max-contrast block (`16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF`) triggers `newBest = 1`!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Two's-Complement Motion Vectors & Systolic Addressing)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 21 · Two's-Complement Motion Vectors] In our `[-8, +7]` search range, what are the 8-bit two's-complement hexadecimal values for `motionX = -8`, `motionX = -5`, and `motionY = +7`?
quiz_questions.hint: For a negative integer `-k` in 8-bit two's complement, compute `256 - k` and convert to hexadecimal (`256 - 8 = 248`, `256 - 5 = 251`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `8'h88` and `8'h85` are sign-magnitude encodings, whereas Verilog arithmetic uses two's complement.
Incorrect — `8'h08` and `8'h05` are positive `+8` and `+5`, while `8'hF7` is `-9`.
Incorrect — `8'hFF` is `-1` and `8'hFA` is `-6`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In 8-bit two's complement (`256 + negative_offset`): `-8 -> 256 - 8 = 248 = 8'hF8`; `-5 -> 256 - 5 = 251 = 8'hFB`; `+7 -> 8'h07`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Systolic Pipeline Latency & Throughput Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 21 · Advanced Systolic Array Timing] Why does a full 256-candidate macroblock search across the 16-PE systolic array take exactly `4,111` clock cycles (`count == 13'h100F`), and what is the throughput in macroblocks/second at `520 MHz`?
options: A) 256 candidates * 256 pixels = 65,536 cycles (7,934 macroblocks/sec)

B) 16 vertical search rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles + 15 Rpipe pipeline fill cycles for PE15 = 4,111 cycles (`7.906 us` per macroblock = `126,489 macroblocks/sec`, or `30.9 frames/sec` for 1024x1024 video!)
C) 16 PEs * 16 rows = 256 cycles
D) 4,095 cycles (`12'hFFF`)
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that all 16 horizontal candidates in a row are computed in parallel across `PE0..PE15` in 256 cycles, but `PE15` receives `R` delayed by 15 `Rpipe` stages!
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `65,536` cycles would be a sequential 1-PE engine; our 16-PE systolic array achieves a 16x speedup!

Correct! `16 rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles`, plus `15` cycles for `Rpipe[0..14]` to reach `PE15` = `4,111 cycles` (`13'h100F`). At `1.923 ns/cycle`, `4,111 * 1.923 ns = 7.906 us` (`126,489 macroblocks/s`).
Incorrect — Each candidate requires accumulating `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, not 16 pixels.
Incorrect — At cycle `4,095`, `PE15` still has 15 pixels left in the `Rpipe` shift register before completing its 256-pixel sum at cycle `4,111`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `4,096 + 15 = 4,111` clock cycles (`13'h100F`). Dividing `520,000,000 Hz / 4,111 cycles = 126,489.9 macroblocks/sec`, which processes `4,096` macroblocks (a full `1024x1024` frame) at `30.88 fps`!

foundation_text: Chapter 10 Sec. 10.4 Foundation Bridge (Page 22): Each grayscale video pixel is an 8-bit unsigned integer `0..255` (`2^8 = 256` levels). Comparing a 16x16 Reference macroblock (`256` pixels) against a 16x16 Search candidate adds 256 absolute differences `|R - S|`. three_methods.method1: Behavior on Page 22 (Page 22: The 16-Bit Non-Saturating Datapath Solution  -  Exact SAD Resolution Up to 65,280): Trace how the 16 Processing Elements (`PE0..PE15`) evaluate 16 horizontal candidates `u in [-8..+7]` in parallel while `R` shifts through `Rpipe[0..14]`.
three_methods.method2: Mathematical & Bit-Width Proof: `SAD(u,v) = sum_{i=0..15} sum_{j=0..15} |R(i,j) - S(i+u, j+v)|`. Bit width required = `ceil(log2(256 * 255 + 1)) = 16 bits` (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`). An 8-bit register (`max 255 = 8'hFF`) overflows on Row 0 whenever average `|R-S| >= 1`!
three_methods.method3: RTL & Hardware Mapping: Each PE needs an 8-bit 2:1 mux (`S1` vs `S2`), an 8-bit absolute difference circuit (`|R - S|`), a 16-bit adder, and a 16-bit DFF accumulator (`Accumulate[15:0]`), feeding a 16:1 mux and 16-bit comparator (`BestDist[15:0]`).

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Ch. 10 SAD Bit-Width & Saturation Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 22 · Bit-Width & Saturation Math (Midterm Q2 Connection)] What is the maximum possible SAD value for a 16x16 macroblock of 8-bit pixels (`0..255`), and how many bits are required to represent it without saturation or wrap-around?
options: A) Max SAD = 255 (8'hFF); requires 8 bits.
B) Max SAD = 4,080 (16'h0FF0); requires 12 bits.
C) Max SAD = 65,280 (16'hFF00 = 256 pixels * 255 max diff); requires 16 bits (with 16'hFFFF = 65,535 reserved as the initial BestDist).
D) Max SAD = 65,536; requires 17 bits.
quiz_questions.hint: Multiply the total number of pixels in a 16x16 macroblock (`16 * 16 = 256`) by the maximum possible 8-bit pixel difference (`|255 - 0| = 255`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `255 (8'hFF)` is the maximum difference of a SINGLE pixel, not the sum across 256 pixels!
Incorrect — `4,080 (16 * 255)` is the maximum SAD of a single 16-pixel row (`Row 0`), not all 16 rows (`256` pixels).
Correct! `256 pixels * 255 max diff = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`) prevents overflow and leaves `16'hFFFF` as a valid sentinel initial value for `BestDist`!
Incorrect — `65,280` fits comfortably inside 16 unsigned bits (`0..65,535`), so a 17th bit is unnecessary.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: C) `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, each with max difference `|0 - 255| = 255`. Thus `SAD_max = 256 * 255 = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits allows `BestDist` to initialize to `16'hFFFF (65,535)` so even a max-contrast block (`16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF`) triggers `newBest = 1`!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Two's-Complement Motion Vectors & Systolic Addressing)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 22 · Two's-Complement Motion Vectors] In our `[-8, +7]` search range, what are the 8-bit two's-complement hexadecimal values for `motionX = -8`, `motionX = -5`, and `motionY = +7`?
quiz_questions.hint: For a negative integer `-k` in 8-bit two's complement, compute `256 - k` and convert to hexadecimal (`256 - 8 = 248`, `256 - 5 = 251`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `8'h88` and `8'h85` are sign-magnitude encodings, whereas Verilog arithmetic uses two's complement.
Incorrect — `8'h08` and `8'h05` are positive `+8` and `+5`, while `8'hF7` is `-9`.
Incorrect — `8'hFF` is `-1` and `8'hFA` is `-6`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In 8-bit two's complement (`256 + negative_offset`): `-8 -> 256 - 8 = 248 = 8'hF8`; `-5 -> 256 - 5 = 251 = 8'hFB`; `+7 -> 8'h07`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Systolic Pipeline Latency & Throughput Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 22 · Advanced Systolic Array Timing] Why does a full 256-candidate macroblock search across the 16-PE systolic array take exactly `4,111` clock cycles (`count == 13'h100F`), and what is the throughput in macroblocks/second at `520 MHz`?
options: A) 256 candidates * 256 pixels = 65,536 cycles (7,934 macroblocks/sec)

B) 16 vertical search rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles + 15 Rpipe pipeline fill cycles for PE15 = 4,111 cycles (`7.906 us` per macroblock = `126,489 macroblocks/sec`, or `30.9 frames/sec` for 1024x1024 video!)
C) 16 PEs * 16 rows = 256 cycles
D) 4,095 cycles (`12'hFFF`)
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that all 16 horizontal candidates in a row are computed in parallel across `PE0..PE15` in 256 cycles, but `PE15` receives `R` delayed by 15 `Rpipe` stages!
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `65,536` cycles would be a sequential 1-PE engine; our 16-PE systolic array achieves a 16x speedup!

Correct! `16 rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles`, plus `15` cycles for `Rpipe[0..14]` to reach `PE15` = `4,111 cycles` (`13'h100F`). At `1.923 ns/cycle`, `4,111 * 1.923 ns = 7.906 us` (`126,489 macroblocks/s`).
Incorrect — Each candidate requires accumulating `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, not 16 pixels.
Incorrect — At cycle `4,095`, `PE15` still has 15 pixels left in the `Rpipe` shift register before completing its 256-pixel sum at cycle `4,111`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `4,096 + 15 = 4,111` clock cycles (`13'h100F`). Dividing `520,000,000 Hz / 4,111 cycles = 126,489.9 macroblocks/sec`, which processes `4,096` macroblocks (a full `1024x1024` frame) at `30.88 fps`!

title: Page 23: [!] TRAP: The 12-Bit Counter Wrap-Around at Cycle 4096 & Terminal Hold Fix! [!]
subtitle: Why Extending count to [12:0] and Holding at 13'h100F (Cycle 4111) Prevents Post-Search Corruption
where_badge: XQUARTZ / SSH MAHMOODI SERVER TERMINAL (`bash` on `926784856@mahmoodi.rcc.at.sfsu.edu`)
v_desc: Ch. 10 Sec. 10.4 SAD Math, 8-Bit Saturation Trap & 16-Bit Theory
trap_notes: RED:[!] CRITICAL BUG IN ORIGINAL 12-BIT CONTROL COUNTER: [!]
Because the last 16 comparisons occur at cycles 4096..4111 (13'h1000..13'h100F), a 12-bit counter
wraps around to 0 at cycle 4096, causing 'if (count < 256) CompStart = 0' to wipe out BestDist!
Widening count to [12:0] and latching 'completed <= 1' at 13'h100F fixes this completely!
code_block: // In module Control (rtl/16bit/top.v):
reg [12:0] count; reg completed;
always @(posedge clock) begin
if (start == 0) begin count <= 13'd0; completed <= 1'b0; end
else if (completed == 1'b0) begin
if (count == 13'h100F) completed <= 1'b1; // Freeze after cycle 4111 (all 256 blocks done)
else count <= count + 13'd1;
end
end
// --- Interactive Hardware Verification of This Architectural Step on mahmoodi ---

TERM_SFSU: [926784856@mahmoodi me_asic_new_v1]$ tcsh -c 'source ./scripts/synopsys_setup.tcl; vcs -full64 -sverilog -debug_access+all rtl/16bit/top.v tb/16bit/top_tb_direct.v -o simv_check && ./simv_check'
OUT_OK:    Cycle 256 (0x0100): CompStart=1, PEready=0x0001 | Cycle 4111 (0x100F): completed=1, BestDist=16'h0000
// --- Comparing 8-Bit Baseline (rtl/8bit/top.v) vs. 16-Bit Non-Saturating Upgrade (rtl/16bit/top.v) ---
01: // In 8-bit PE:  {Carry, AccumulateIn} = Accumulate + difference; if (Carry == 1) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;
02: // In 16-bit PE: AccumulateIn = Accumulate + {8'd0, difference};  // Exact sum up to 256*255 = 65,280 (16'hFF00)
03: // In 8-bit Control:  reg [11:0] count; // Wraps to 0 at cycle 4096 -> resets BestDist during Row 15!
04: // In 16-bit Control: reg [12:0] count; reg completed; // Holds at count == 13'h100F (cycle 4111)!
05: // In 8-bit Comparator:  if (CompStart == 0) BestDist <= 8'hFF;   // Ties when newDist == 8'hFF!
06: // In 16-bit Comparator: if (CompStart == 0) BestDist <= 16'hFFFF; // 16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF is always TRUE!

foundation_text: Chapter 10 Sec. 10.4 Foundation Bridge (Page 23): Each grayscale video pixel is an 8-bit unsigned integer `0..255` (`2^8 = 256` levels). Comparing a 16x16 Reference macroblock (`256` pixels) against a 16x16 Search candidate adds 256 absolute differences `|R - S|`. Since each pixel difference can be up to `255`, the maximum possible sum is `256 * 255 = 65,280` (`16'hFF00`).

three_methods.method1: Behavior on Page 23 (Page 23: [!] TRAP: The 12-Bit Counter Wrap-Around at Cycle 4096 & Terminal Hold Fix! [!]): Trace how the 16 Processing Elements (`PE0..PE15`) evaluate 16 horizontal candidates `u in [-8..+7]` in parallel while `R` shifts through `Rpipe[0..14]`.
three_methods.method2: Mathematical & Bit-Width Proof: `SAD(u,v) = sum_{i=0..15} sum_{j=0..15} |R(i,j) - S(i+u, j+v)|`. Bit width required = `ceil(log2(256 * 255 + 1)) = 16 bits` (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`). An 8-bit register (`max 255 = 8'hFF`) overflows on Row 0 whenever average `|R-S| >= 1`!
three_methods.method3: RTL & Hardware Mapping: Each PE needs an 8-bit 2:1 mux (`S1` vs `S2`), an 8-bit absolute difference circuit (`|R - S|`), a 16-bit adder, and a 16-bit DFF accumulator (`Accumulate[15:0]`), feeding a 16:1 mux and 16-bit comparator (`BestDist[15:0]`).

quiz_questions.q: [Page 23 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 23's combined one-liner, why do we execute `snap_step "page023_trap_12_bit_counter" 'grep -En -C 4 "13\'h100F|comp` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Loads the telemetry bridge and wraps the page's command sequence in the Expected-Outcome Verifier. Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 23's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `snap_step "page023_trap_12_bit_counter" 'grep -En -C 4 "13\'` performs: Loads the telemetry bridge and wraps the page's command sequence in the Expected-Outcome Verifier. And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 23's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Ch. 10 SAD Bit-Width & Saturation Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 23 · Bit-Width & Saturation Math (Midterm Q2 Connection)] What is the maximum possible SAD value for a 16x16 macroblock of 8-bit pixels (`0..255`), and how many bits are required to represent it without saturation or wrap-around?
options: A) Max SAD = 255 (8'hFF); requires 8 bits.
B) Max SAD = 4,080 (16'h0FF0); requires 12 bits.
C) Max SAD = 65,280 (16'hFF00 = 256 pixels * 255 max diff); requires 16 bits (with 16'hFFFF = 65,535 reserved as the initial BestDist).
D) Max SAD = 65,536; requires 17 bits.
quiz_questions.hint: Multiply the total number of pixels in a 16x16 macroblock (`16 * 16 = 256`) by the maximum possible 8-bit pixel difference (`|255 - 0| = 255`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `255 (8'hFF)` is the maximum difference of a SINGLE pixel, not the sum across 256 pixels!
Incorrect — `4,080 (16 * 255)` is the maximum SAD of a single 16-pixel row (`Row 0`), not all 16 rows (`256` pixels).
Correct! `256 pixels * 255 max diff = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits (`max 65,535 = 16'hFFFF`) prevents overflow and leaves `16'hFFFF` as a valid sentinel initial value for `BestDist`!
Incorrect — `65,280` fits comfortably inside 16 unsigned bits (`0..65,535`), so a 17th bit is unnecessary.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: C) `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, each with max difference `|0 - 255| = 255`. Thus `SAD_max = 256 * 255 = 65,280 = 16'hFF00`. Using 16 bits allows `BestDist` to initialize to `16'hFFFF (65,535)` so even a max-contrast block (`16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF`) triggers `newBest = 1`!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Two's-Complement Motion Vectors & Systolic Addressing)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 23 · Two's-Complement Motion Vectors] In our `[-8, +7]` search range, what are the 8-bit two's-complement hexadecimal values for `motionX = -8`, `motionX = -5`, and `motionY = +7`?
quiz_questions.hint: For a negative integer `-k` in 8-bit two's complement, compute `256 - k` and convert to hexadecimal (`256 - 8 = 248`, `256 - 5 = 251`).
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `8'h88` and `8'h85` are sign-magnitude encodings, whereas Verilog arithmetic uses two's complement.
Incorrect — `8'h08` and `8'h05` are positive `+8` and `+5`, while `8'hF7` is `-9`.
Incorrect — `8'hFF` is `-1` and `8'hFA` is `-6`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In 8-bit two's complement (`256 + negative_offset`): `-8 -> 256 - 8 = 248 = 8'hF8`; `-5 -> 256 - 5 = 251 = 8'hFB`; `+7 -> 8'h07`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Systolic Pipeline Latency & Throughput Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 23 · Advanced Systolic Array Timing] Why does a full 256-candidate macroblock search across the 16-PE systolic array take exactly `4,111` clock cycles (`count == 13'h100F`), and what is the throughput in macroblocks/second at `520 MHz`?
options: A) 256 candidates * 256 pixels = 65,536 cycles (7,934 macroblocks/sec)

B) 16 vertical search rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles + 15 Rpipe pipeline fill cycles for PE15 = 4,111 cycles (`7.906 us` per macroblock = `126,489 macroblocks/sec`, or `30.9 frames/sec` for 1024x1024 video!)
C) 16 PEs * 16 rows = 256 cycles
D) 4,095 cycles (`12'hFFF`)
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that all 16 horizontal candidates in a row are computed in parallel across `PE0..PE15` in 256 cycles, but `PE15` receives `R` delayed by 15 `Rpipe` stages!
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — `65,536` cycles would be a sequential 1-PE engine; our 16-PE systolic array achieves a 16x speedup!

Correct! `16 rows * 256 cycles/row = 4,096 cycles`, plus `15` cycles for `Rpipe[0..14]` to reach `PE15` = `4,111 cycles` (`13'h100F`). At `1.923 ns/cycle`, `4,111 * 1.923 ns = 7.906 us` (`126,489 macroblocks/s`).
Incorrect — Each candidate requires accumulating `16 * 16 = 256` pixels, not 16 pixels.
Incorrect — At cycle `4,095`, `PE15` still has 15 pixels left in the `Rpipe` shift register before completing its 256-pixel sum at cycle `4,111`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `4,096 + 15 = 4,111` clock cycles (`13'h100F`). Dividing `520,000,000 Hz / 4,111 cycles = 126,489.9 macroblocks/sec`, which processes `4,096` macroblocks (a full `1024x1024` frame) at `30.88 fps`!
