quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 2 · Easy-Medium (Hands-On Command Mechanics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 34 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 34's combined one-liner, why do we execute `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 34's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 34's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 34 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 34 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 34 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 2 · Easy-Medium (Hands-On Command Mechanics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 35 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 35's combined one-liner, why do we execute `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/rtl/16bit ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit ~/me_asi` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 35's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/rtl/16bit ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bi` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 35's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 35 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 35 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 35 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).

options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 36's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.

quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.

quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 36's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 36 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 36 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 36 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.

quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 37's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 37 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 37 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 37 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 38's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/rtl/16bit ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bi` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 38 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 38 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 38 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 2 · Easy-Medium (Hands-On Command Mechanics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 39 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 39's combined one-liner, why do we execute `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 39's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 39's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 39 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 39 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 39 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 2 · Easy-Medium (Hands-On Command Mechanics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 40 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 40's combined one-liner, why do we execute `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 40's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 40's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 40 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 40 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 40 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 2 · Easy-Medium (Hands-On Command Mechanics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 41 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 41's combined one-liner, why do we execute `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/rtl/16bit ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit ~/me_asi` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 41's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/rtl/16bit ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bi` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 41's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 41 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 41 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 41 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.q: [Page 42 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 42's combined one-liner, why do we execute `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 42's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/tb/16bit` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 42's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 42 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 42 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 42 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.q: [Page 43 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 43 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 43 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 44 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 44 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 44 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 2 · Easy-Medium (Hands-On Command Mechanics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 45 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 45's combined one-liner, why do we execute `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/{rtl/8bit,tb/8bit,logs,waveforms}` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 45's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/{rtl/8bit,tb/8bit,logs,waveforms}` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 45's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 45 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 45 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 45 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.q: [Page 46 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 46's combined one-liner, why do we execute `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/scripts/verdi_nwave ~/me_asic_new_v1/wavefor` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 46's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/scripts/verdi_nwave ~/me_asic_new_` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
