quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 46 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 46 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 46 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 2 · Easy-Medium (Hands-On Command Mechanics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 47 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 47's combined one-liner, why do we execute `nl -ba ~/me_asic_new_v1/scripts/verdi_nwave/fig7_orig8bit_row1.tcl` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Launches Synopsys Verdi nWave to inspect Fast Signal Database (`.fsdb`) waveforms in hexadecimal radix. Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 47's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `nl -ba ~/me_asic_new_v1/scripts/verdi_nwave/fig7_orig8bit_ro` performs: Launches Synopsys Verdi nWave to inspect Fast Signal Database (`.fsdb`) waveforms in hexadecimal radix. And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 47's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 47 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 47 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 47 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 2 · Easy-Medium (Hands-On Command Mechanics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 48 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 48's combined one-liner, why do we execute `nl -ba ~/me_asic_new_v1/scripts/verdi_nwave/fig8_orig8bit_complete.tcl` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Launches Synopsys Verdi nWave to inspect Fast Signal Database (`.fsdb`) waveforms in hexadecimal radix. Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 48's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `nl -ba ~/me_asic_new_v1/scripts/verdi_nwave/fig8_orig8bit_co` performs: Launches Synopsys Verdi nWave to inspect Fast Signal Database (`.fsdb`) waveforms in hexadecimal radix. And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 48's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 48 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 48 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 48 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 2 · Easy-Medium (Hands-On Command Mechanics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 49 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 49's combined one-liner, why do we execute `mkdir -p ~/motion-estimator-asic-lab-notebook-2026/practice_from_scrat` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 49's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/motion-estimator-asic-lab-notebook-2026/practice_` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 49's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 49 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 49 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 49 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 2 · Easy-Medium (Hands-On Command Mechanics)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 50 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 50's combined one-liner, why do we execute `mkdir -p ~/motion-estimator-asic-lab-notebook-2026/practice_from_scrat` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 50's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/motion-estimator-asic-lab-notebook-2026/practice_` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 50's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 50 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 50 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 50 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 51 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 51 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.

choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).

quiz_questions.q: [Page 51 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 52's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/motion-estimator-asic-lab-notebook-2026/practice_` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 52's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation — F1)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 52 · 520 MHz Testbench Clock Generation] In `top_tb.v` with `` `timescale 1ns/10ps ``, how is a 520 MHz clock (`T_clk = 1.923 ns`) generated in Verilog?
options: A) `always #1.923 clock = ~clock;`
B) `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` (since a full clock period has two half-cycles: `2 * 0.9615 ns = 1.923 ns = 1 / 520 MHz`).
C) `always #520 clock = ~clock;`
D) `assign clock = 1'b1;`
quiz_questions.hint: Remember that `clock = ~clock` only flips the signal once (either `0->1` or `1->0`). How many inversions make 1 full clock period `T_clk = 1.923 ns`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Delaying `#1.923` per half-cycle makes the full period `2 * 1.923 = 3.846 ns` (`260 MHz`, half the required frequency!).
Correct! Two half-periods of `0.9615 ns` equal one full period of `1.923 ns` (`1 / 1.923 ns = 520.02 MHz`).
Incorrect — `#520` under `1ns` timescale waits `520 ns` per half-cycle (`T_clk = 1,040 ns = 0.96 MHz`).
Incorrect — Holding `clock = 1'b1` produces zero rising edges, so no sequential logic ever advances.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) `clock = ~clock` inverts the clock twice per period (rising edge + falling edge). Half of `1.923 ns` is `0.9615 ns`, so `always #0.9615 clock = ~clock;` produces `T_clk = 1.923 ns (520 MHz)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (Verdi nWave Waveform Forensics — Fig 7 vs. Fig 9)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 52 · Verdi nWave Waveform Analysis] In Figure 7 (`V9_fig7_orig8bit_row1_nWave.png`, 8-bit baseline) vs. Figure 9 (`V9_fig9_16bit_saturation_row1_nWave.png`, 16-bit upgrade) at `count = 13'h0100` (end of candidate 0), what happens to `BestDist` and `newBest` under max-contrast input?
options: A) In 8-bit (Fig 7), `pe0.Accumulate = 8'hFF` is NOT `< BestDist (8'hFF)` so `newBest = 0`; in 16-bit (Fig 9), `pe0.Accumulate = 16'hFF00 (65,280) < BestDist (16'hFFFF = 65,535)` so `newBest = 1` and `BestDist` updates to `16'hFF00`!
B) Both 8-bit and 16-bit output `BestDist = 0`.
C) 8-bit updates `BestDist` to `8'h00`.
D) `newBest` is only used during synthesis.
quiz_questions.hint: Inspect the comparator equation `newBest = (pe_sad < BestDist)` at `count = 13'h0100` (`t = 499.0 ns`) when `pe0` finishes its 256th pixel.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! That exact cycle at `count = 13'h0100` is the visual smoking gun comparing V1 (8-bit fail, `8'hFF < 8'hFF` is false) and V2–V9 (16-bit pass, `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` is true).
Incorrect — Under max-contrast input (`|R-S| = 255`), the distortion is maximal (`65,280 = 16'hFF00`), not zero.
Incorrect — The 8-bit PE saturates at `8'hFF` (`if (AccumulateCarry) AccumulateIn = 8'hFF;`) rather than wrapping to `8'h00`.
Incorrect — `newBest` is the active-high enable signal inside `comp.v` that latches `BestDist`, `motionX`, and `motionY` during simulation and hardware operation.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In V1 (Fig 7), `8'hFF < 8'hFF` evaluates to `0`, leaving `motionX/Y = xx`. In V2 (Fig 9), `16'hFF00 < 16'hFFFF` evaluates to `1`, latching `BestDist = 16'hFF00` and `(motionX, motionY) = (-8, -8)`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (+1 LSB Surgical Boundary Test `16'h0100`)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 52 · Surgical Testbench Design] Why did we design Testbench #2 (`top_tb.v`) so that the winning candidate at `(-5, +7)` has every pixel perturbed by exactly `+1` LSB (`|R - S| = 1` across all 256 pixels, yielding `BestDist = 16'h0100 = 256`), while all other candidates differ by `>= 2` LSBs?
options: A) Because `256 (16'h0100)` is the exact mathematical boundary (`255 + 1`) where an 8-bit unsigned accumulator overflows/saturates to `8'hFF (255)`! Thus `BestDist == 16'h0100` with `(motionX, motionY) == (8'hFB, 8'h07)` simultaneously proves bit-8 (`Accumulate[8]`) carry propagation and signed coordinate decoding.
B) Because `+1` LSB makes simulation run 10x faster.
C) Because `16'h0100` equals `100` in decimal.
D) Because `RMEM` can only store `+1`.
quiz_questions.hint: Convert hexadecimal `16'h0100` to decimal (`1 * 16^2 = 256`) and compare `256` against the maximum value of an 8-bit unsigned integer (`255`).
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `256 = 16'h0100` is the very first integer (`255 + 1`) that requires bit 8 (`2^8`) of the 16-bit accumulator, making it the sharpest possible boundary test between 8-bit (`0xFF`) and 16-bit (`0x0100`) precision!
Incorrect — Simulation runtime depends on the number of clock cycles (`4,111`), not the numeric pixel values in `SMEM`.
Incorrect — `16'h0100` in hexadecimal is `1 * 256 = 256` in decimal (not `100`).
Incorrect — `RMEM` stores arbitrary 8-bit grayscale intensities `0x00..0xFF`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) `256 pixels * 1 LSB/pixel = 256_10 = 16'h0100`. In V1 (8-bit), `256` clamped to `255 (8'hFF)`. Observing `BestDist = 16'h0100`, `motionX = 8'hFB (-5)`, `motionY = 8'h07 (+7)` proves bit-accurate 9th-bit carry into the upper byte `[15:8]`.

01: # Course Project Specification: Clock = 520 MHz (1.923 ns), I/O Delay = 0.5 ns, Uncertainty = 0.2 ns
02: create_clock -name clock -period 1.923 [get_ports clock]   ;# 1000 / 1.923 = 520.02 MHz
03: set_clock_uncertainty 0.2 [get_clocks clock]               ;# 200 ps jitter + skew margin
04: # Constrain all 25 data/control input ports (exclude clock port itself!):

06: # Constrain all 60 output ports (BestDist[15:0], motionX[7:0], motionY[7:0], AddressR/S1/S2):
07: set_output_delay 0.5 -clock clock [all_outputs]
08: # Note: Reference (ROM_R) and Search (ROM_S) memories are EXCLUDED from top.v synthesis!

quiz_questions.q: [Page 53 · Hands-On Lab Mechanics] In Page 53's combined one-liner, why do we execute `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/common/sdc ~/me_asic_new_v1/constraints` and chain subsequent sub-commands using the logical AND operator (`&&`) inside `snap_step`?
options: A) Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). Chaining with `&&` guarantees short-circuit safety (the next sub-command only runs if exit_code == 0), while `snap_step` captures the terminal log, renders a screenshot, and verifies Page 53's expected output markers.
B) The `&&` operator runs all commands in reverse order from right to left.
C) It deletes the main project repository on GitHub.
D) It bypasses all Synopsys license checks by disabling the system clock.
quiz_questions.hint: Recall how UNIX shells (`zsh` and `bash`) evaluate `cmd1 && cmd2`: does `cmd2` execute if `cmd1` returns a non-zero error code?
choice_diagnostics: Correct! `mkdir -p ~/me_asic_new_v1/common/sdc ~/me_asic_new_v1/constr` performs: Creates isolated directory hierarchy (without failing if directories already exist). And `&&` stops immediately if any sub-command fails so the `:8788` Auto-Debugger can pinpoint and repair the exact failing step.
Incorrect — `&&` evaluates strictly left-to-right, executing the right-hand command only if the left-hand command returned exit code `0`.
Incorrect — `snap_step` strictly isolates all work inside your manual practice workspace (`~/Developer/motion-estimator-14nm-asic-manual` and `manual-practice-macbook-air`), never touching `main`.
Incorrect — Shell operators control process execution flow in the operating system and have no effect on EDA license daemons.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) In UNIX shells (`zsh`/`bash`), `cmd1 && cmd2` short-circuits immediately on any non-zero exit code (`$? != 0`). Wrapping the chain inside `snap_step` logs stdout/stderr, renders the PNG proof, and checks Page 53's `required_markers`.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Midterm Q3/Q4/Q9 — Setup Slack & F_max Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 53 · STA Setup & Hold Equations] Our 14nm Motion Estimator achieves Setup WNS = `+0.22 ns` in the worst-case slow corner (`ss0p72vm40c`) at `T_clk = 1.923 ns` (520 MHz). What is the longest critical-path total arrival + setup + uncertainty time in `ss0p72vm40c`, and what is the maximum achievable clock frequency?
options: A) Critical path total time = `1.923 ns - 0.22 ns = 1.703 ns`; max frequency `f_max = 1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz`.
B) Critical path total time = `1.923 ns + 0.22 ns = 2.143 ns`; max frequency = `466 MHz`.
C) Critical path total time = `0.22 ns`; max frequency = `4.5 GHz`.
D) Setup WNS does not affect maximum frequency.
quiz_questions.hint: Use the fundamental Setup Slack identity: `Slack_setup = T_clk - T_path_total`. Solve for `T_path_total = T_clk - Slack_setup`, then compute `f_max = 1 / T_path_total`.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! Positive slack `+0.22 ns` means the critical path finished `0.22 ns` BEFORE the `1.923 ns` deadline (`1.923 - 0.22 = 1.703 ns`), allowing operation up to `1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz`!
Incorrect — Adding `+0.22 ns` corresponds to a NEGATIVE slack violation (`-0.22 ns`), whereas our slack is positive (`+0.22 ns`).
Incorrect — `0.22 ns` is the spare timing margin (slack), not the path delay.
Incorrect — Setup WNS directly determines the minimum safe clock period `T_clk,min` and therefore `f_max`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) Since `Slack_setup = T_clk - T_path_total = +0.22 ns`, the critical path takes `1.923 - 0.22 = 1.703 ns`, meaning the routed 14nm chip can run up to `1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz` even in the slowest `0.72V SS` corner!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (14nm Physical DRC Closure & M7 Clock Routing Rule)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 53 · 14nm Physical DRC & CTS Closure] Why did constraining Clock Tree Synthesis to metal layers `M2..M7` (`set_clock_routing_rules -net_type root -max_routing_layer M7`) eliminate the upper-metal DRC violations in standalone Synopsys IC Validator (`icv`)?
options: A) Because `M8` and `M9` are thick top-level power/global layers with wide minimum-spacing and fat-wire rules (`M8.S.6`, `M9.S.6`); keeping high-fanout clock tree branches on `M2..M7` avoids wide-metal stub spacing conflicts and achieves `0 / 242` DRC errors.
B) Because `M7` has zero electrical resistance.
C) Because `icv` only checks `M1`.
D) Because `M8` is made of polysilicon.
quiz_questions.hint: Compare the physical pitch and spacing rules of intermediate signal routing layers (`M2..M7`) versus top-level thick power/global distribution layers (`M8, M9`) in a 14nm FinFET BEOL stack.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! In `SAED14nm`, `M8/M9` carry the PG mesh straps and enforce wide-metal spacing rules (`M8.S.6`, `M9.S.6`). Restricting CTS to `M2..M7` eliminates all upper-metal stub conflicts (`0 / 242` DRC violations).
Incorrect — All copper metal layers have finite sheet resistance `R_s`.
Incorrect — Standalone `icv` evaluates all 242 foundry deck rules across FEOL (FinFET active/gate) and BEOL (`M1..M9` and vias).
Incorrect — `M8` is an upper back-end-of-line (BEOL) copper interconnect layer, not front-end polysilicon.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) Routing clock nets up to `M7` leaves `M8/M9` clean for power/top routing and resolves all 242 SAED14nm deck rules with `0` violations.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Midterm Q3/Q5/Q10 — Same-Edge Hold Physics Across PVT Corners)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 53 · Advanced Multi-Corner STA Physics] Suppose a classmate sees a Hold violation (`Hold WNS = -0.08 ns`) in PrimeTime at the `ff0p88v125c` (Fast-Fast `0.88V`) corner and proposes lowering the clock frequency from `520 MHz` (`1.923 ns`) down to `250 MHz` (`4.000 ns`) to fix it. Based on Midterm Q3 & Q10, will lowering `f_clk` fix the hold violation, and what is the true physical fix?
options: A) Yes, doubling the clock period adds `+2.077 ns` to Hold Slack.

B) No! Hold is checked on the SAME rising clock edge (`Slack_hold = [t_CQ,min + t_logic,min] - [t_hold,max + t_skew]`), which does NOT contain `T_clk`! Lowering frequency has zero effect on hold slack; the true fix is inserting non-inverting delay buffers (`set_fix_hold`) on the short contamination path to increase `t_logic,min` by >= `0.08 ns`.
C) Yes, because hold violations only happen above 500 MHz.
D) No, the only fix is deleting the flip-flop.
quiz_questions.hint: Write down the Hold Slack equation from Midterm Q3 / Q5 / Q10: does the clock period `T_clk` appear anywhere in `(t_CQ,min + t_logic,min) - (t_hold,max + t_skew)`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Adding `+2.077 ns` to `T_clk` increases SETUP slack by `+2.077 ns`, but changes HOLD slack by `0.000 ns`!

Correct! Because Hold checks that a launching DFF does not overwrite a capturing DFF on the SAME clock edge (`t = 0`), `T_clk` cancels out completely. Only adding minimum path delay (delay buffers via `set_fix_hold`) or reducing clock skew fixes a hold violation!
Incorrect — Even a `1 Hz` (`T_clk = 1 second`) clock will fail Hold if `t_CQ,min + t_logic,min < t_hold + t_skew` on the active clock edge!
Incorrect — Deleting pipeline flip-flops breaks the synchronous systolic architecture.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) Directly proven in Midterm Q3, Q5, and Q10: `Slack_hold = (t_CQ,min + t_logic,min) - (t_hold,max + t_skew)` is independent of `T_clk`. In Fusion Compiler / PrimeTime, `set_fix_hold` inserts small delay cells along fast paths (such as direct `Rpipe` shift wires) so `Slack_hold >= 0.00 ns` across all 3 corners.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Midterm Q3/Q4/Q9 — Setup Slack & F_max Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 54 · STA Setup & Hold Equations] Our 14nm Motion Estimator achieves Setup WNS = `+0.22 ns` in the worst-case slow corner (`ss0p72vm40c`) at `T_clk = 1.923 ns` (520 MHz). What is the longest critical-path total arrival + setup + uncertainty time in `ss0p72vm40c`, and what is the maximum achievable clock frequency?
options: A) Critical path total time = `1.923 ns - 0.22 ns = 1.703 ns`; max frequency `f_max = 1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz`.
B) Critical path total time = `1.923 ns + 0.22 ns = 2.143 ns`; max frequency = `466 MHz`.
C) Critical path total time = `0.22 ns`; max frequency = `4.5 GHz`.
D) Setup WNS does not affect maximum frequency.
quiz_questions.hint: Use the fundamental Setup Slack identity: `Slack_setup = T_clk - T_path_total`. Solve for `T_path_total = T_clk - Slack_setup`, then compute `f_max = 1 / T_path_total`.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! Positive slack `+0.22 ns` means the critical path finished `0.22 ns` BEFORE the `1.923 ns` deadline (`1.923 - 0.22 = 1.703 ns`), allowing operation up to `1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz`!
Incorrect — Adding `+0.22 ns` corresponds to a NEGATIVE slack violation (`-0.22 ns`), whereas our slack is positive (`+0.22 ns`).
Incorrect — `0.22 ns` is the spare timing margin (slack), not the path delay.
Incorrect — Setup WNS directly determines the minimum safe clock period `T_clk,min` and therefore `f_max`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) Since `Slack_setup = T_clk - T_path_total = +0.22 ns`, the critical path takes `1.923 - 0.22 = 1.703 ns`, meaning the routed 14nm chip can run up to `1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz` even in the slowest `0.72V SS` corner!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (14nm Physical DRC Closure & M7 Clock Routing Rule)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 54 · 14nm Physical DRC & CTS Closure] Why did constraining Clock Tree Synthesis to metal layers `M2..M7` (`set_clock_routing_rules -net_type root -max_routing_layer M7`) eliminate the upper-metal DRC violations in standalone Synopsys IC Validator (`icv`)?
options: A) Because `M8` and `M9` are thick top-level power/global layers with wide minimum-spacing and fat-wire rules (`M8.S.6`, `M9.S.6`); keeping high-fanout clock tree branches on `M2..M7` avoids wide-metal stub spacing conflicts and achieves `0 / 242` DRC errors.
B) Because `M7` has zero electrical resistance.
C) Because `icv` only checks `M1`.
D) Because `M8` is made of polysilicon.
quiz_questions.hint: Compare the physical pitch and spacing rules of intermediate signal routing layers (`M2..M7`) versus top-level thick power/global distribution layers (`M8, M9`) in a 14nm FinFET BEOL stack.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! In `SAED14nm`, `M8/M9` carry the PG mesh straps and enforce wide-metal spacing rules (`M8.S.6`, `M9.S.6`). Restricting CTS to `M2..M7` eliminates all upper-metal stub conflicts (`0 / 242` DRC violations).
Incorrect — All copper metal layers have finite sheet resistance `R_s`.
Incorrect — Standalone `icv` evaluates all 242 foundry deck rules across FEOL (FinFET active/gate) and BEOL (`M1..M9` and vias).
Incorrect — `M8` is an upper back-end-of-line (BEOL) copper interconnect layer, not front-end polysilicon.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) Routing clock nets up to `M7` leaves `M8/M9` clean for power/top routing and resolves all 242 SAED14nm deck rules with `0` violations.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Midterm Q3/Q5/Q10 — Same-Edge Hold Physics Across PVT Corners)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 54 · Advanced Multi-Corner STA Physics] Suppose a classmate sees a Hold violation (`Hold WNS = -0.08 ns`) in PrimeTime at the `ff0p88v125c` (Fast-Fast `0.88V`) corner and proposes lowering the clock frequency from `520 MHz` (`1.923 ns`) down to `250 MHz` (`4.000 ns`) to fix it. Based on Midterm Q3 & Q10, will lowering `f_clk` fix the hold violation, and what is the true physical fix?
options: A) Yes, doubling the clock period adds `+2.077 ns` to Hold Slack.

B) No! Hold is checked on the SAME rising clock edge (`Slack_hold = [t_CQ,min + t_logic,min] - [t_hold,max + t_skew]`), which does NOT contain `T_clk`! Lowering frequency has zero effect on hold slack; the true fix is inserting non-inverting delay buffers (`set_fix_hold`) on the short contamination path to increase `t_logic,min` by >= `0.08 ns`.
C) Yes, because hold violations only happen above 500 MHz.
D) No, the only fix is deleting the flip-flop.
quiz_questions.hint: Write down the Hold Slack equation from Midterm Q3 / Q5 / Q10: does the clock period `T_clk` appear anywhere in `(t_CQ,min + t_logic,min) - (t_hold,max + t_skew)`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Adding `+2.077 ns` to `T_clk` increases SETUP slack by `+2.077 ns`, but changes HOLD slack by `0.000 ns`!

Correct! Because Hold checks that a launching DFF does not overwrite a capturing DFF on the SAME clock edge (`t = 0`), `T_clk` cancels out completely. Only adding minimum path delay (delay buffers via `set_fix_hold`) or reducing clock skew fixes a hold violation!
Incorrect — Even a `1 Hz` (`T_clk = 1 second`) clock will fail Hold if `t_CQ,min + t_logic,min < t_hold + t_skew` on the active clock edge!
Incorrect — Deleting pipeline flip-flops breaks the synchronous systolic architecture.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) Directly proven in Midterm Q3, Q5, and Q10: `Slack_hold = (t_CQ,min + t_logic,min) - (t_hold,max + t_skew)` is independent of `T_clk`. In Fusion Compiler / PrimeTime, `set_fix_hold` inserts small delay cells along fast paths (such as direct `Rpipe` shift wires) so `Slack_hold >= 0.00 ns` across all 3 corners.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Midterm Q3/Q4/Q9 — Setup Slack & F_max Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 55 · STA Setup & Hold Equations] Our 14nm Motion Estimator achieves Setup WNS = `+0.22 ns` in the worst-case slow corner (`ss0p72vm40c`) at `T_clk = 1.923 ns` (520 MHz). What is the longest critical-path total arrival + setup + uncertainty time in `ss0p72vm40c`, and what is the maximum achievable clock frequency?
options: A) Critical path total time = `1.923 ns - 0.22 ns = 1.703 ns`; max frequency `f_max = 1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz`.
B) Critical path total time = `1.923 ns + 0.22 ns = 2.143 ns`; max frequency = `466 MHz`.
C) Critical path total time = `0.22 ns`; max frequency = `4.5 GHz`.
D) Setup WNS does not affect maximum frequency.
quiz_questions.hint: Use the fundamental Setup Slack identity: `Slack_setup = T_clk - T_path_total`. Solve for `T_path_total = T_clk - Slack_setup`, then compute `f_max = 1 / T_path_total`.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! Positive slack `+0.22 ns` means the critical path finished `0.22 ns` BEFORE the `1.923 ns` deadline (`1.923 - 0.22 = 1.703 ns`), allowing operation up to `1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz`!
Incorrect — Adding `+0.22 ns` corresponds to a NEGATIVE slack violation (`-0.22 ns`), whereas our slack is positive (`+0.22 ns`).
Incorrect — `0.22 ns` is the spare timing margin (slack), not the path delay.
Incorrect — Setup WNS directly determines the minimum safe clock period `T_clk,min` and therefore `f_max`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) Since `Slack_setup = T_clk - T_path_total = +0.22 ns`, the critical path takes `1.923 - 0.22 = 1.703 ns`, meaning the routed 14nm chip can run up to `1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz` even in the slowest `0.72V SS` corner!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (14nm Physical DRC Closure & M7 Clock Routing Rule)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 55 · 14nm Physical DRC & CTS Closure] Why did constraining Clock Tree Synthesis to metal layers `M2..M7` (`set_clock_routing_rules -net_type root -max_routing_layer M7`) eliminate the upper-metal DRC violations in standalone Synopsys IC Validator (`icv`)?
options: A) Because `M8` and `M9` are thick top-level power/global layers with wide minimum-spacing and fat-wire rules (`M8.S.6`, `M9.S.6`); keeping high-fanout clock tree branches on `M2..M7` avoids wide-metal stub spacing conflicts and achieves `0 / 242` DRC errors.
B) Because `M7` has zero electrical resistance.
C) Because `icv` only checks `M1`.
D) Because `M8` is made of polysilicon.
quiz_questions.hint: Compare the physical pitch and spacing rules of intermediate signal routing layers (`M2..M7`) versus top-level thick power/global distribution layers (`M8, M9`) in a 14nm FinFET BEOL stack.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! In `SAED14nm`, `M8/M9` carry the PG mesh straps and enforce wide-metal spacing rules (`M8.S.6`, `M9.S.6`). Restricting CTS to `M2..M7` eliminates all upper-metal stub conflicts (`0 / 242` DRC violations).
Incorrect — All copper metal layers have finite sheet resistance `R_s`.
Incorrect — Standalone `icv` evaluates all 242 foundry deck rules across FEOL (FinFET active/gate) and BEOL (`M1..M9` and vias).
Incorrect — `M8` is an upper back-end-of-line (BEOL) copper interconnect layer, not front-end polysilicon.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) Routing clock nets up to `M7` leaves `M8/M9` clean for power/top routing and resolves all 242 SAED14nm deck rules with `0` violations.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Midterm Q3/Q5/Q10 — Same-Edge Hold Physics Across PVT Corners)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 55 · Advanced Multi-Corner STA Physics] Suppose a classmate sees a Hold violation (`Hold WNS = -0.08 ns`) in PrimeTime at the `ff0p88v125c` (Fast-Fast `0.88V`) corner and proposes lowering the clock frequency from `520 MHz` (`1.923 ns`) down to `250 MHz` (`4.000 ns`) to fix it. Based on Midterm Q3 & Q10, will lowering `f_clk` fix the hold violation, and what is the true physical fix?
options: A) Yes, doubling the clock period adds `+2.077 ns` to Hold Slack.

B) No! Hold is checked on the SAME rising clock edge (`Slack_hold = [t_CQ,min + t_logic,min] - [t_hold,max + t_skew]`), which does NOT contain `T_clk`! Lowering frequency has zero effect on hold slack; the true fix is inserting non-inverting delay buffers (`set_fix_hold`) on the short contamination path to increase `t_logic,min` by >= `0.08 ns`.
C) Yes, because hold violations only happen above 500 MHz.
D) No, the only fix is deleting the flip-flop.
quiz_questions.hint: Write down the Hold Slack equation from Midterm Q3 / Q5 / Q10: does the clock period `T_clk` appear anywhere in `(t_CQ,min + t_logic,min) - (t_hold,max + t_skew)`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Adding `+2.077 ns` to `T_clk` increases SETUP slack by `+2.077 ns`, but changes HOLD slack by `0.000 ns`!

Correct! Because Hold checks that a launching DFF does not overwrite a capturing DFF on the SAME clock edge (`t = 0`), `T_clk` cancels out completely. Only adding minimum path delay (delay buffers via `set_fix_hold`) or reducing clock skew fixes a hold violation!
Incorrect — Even a `1 Hz` (`T_clk = 1 second`) clock will fail Hold if `t_CQ,min + t_logic,min < t_hold + t_skew` on the active clock edge!
Incorrect — Deleting pipeline flip-flops breaks the synchronous systolic architecture.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) Directly proven in Midterm Q3, Q5, and Q10: `Slack_hold = (t_CQ,min + t_logic,min) - (t_hold,max + t_skew)` is independent of `T_clk`. In Fusion Compiler / PrimeTime, `set_fix_hold` inserts small delay cells along fast paths (such as direct `Rpipe` shift wires) so `Slack_hold >= 0.00 ns` across all 3 corners.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Midterm Q3/Q4/Q9 — Setup Slack & F_max Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 56 · STA Setup & Hold Equations] Our 14nm Motion Estimator achieves Setup WNS = `+0.22 ns` in the worst-case slow corner (`ss0p72vm40c`) at `T_clk = 1.923 ns` (520 MHz). What is the longest critical-path total arrival + setup + uncertainty time in `ss0p72vm40c`, and what is the maximum achievable clock frequency?
options: A) Critical path total time = `1.923 ns - 0.22 ns = 1.703 ns`; max frequency `f_max = 1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz`.
B) Critical path total time = `1.923 ns + 0.22 ns = 2.143 ns`; max frequency = `466 MHz`.
C) Critical path total time = `0.22 ns`; max frequency = `4.5 GHz`.
D) Setup WNS does not affect maximum frequency.
quiz_questions.hint: Use the fundamental Setup Slack identity: `Slack_setup = T_clk - T_path_total`. Solve for `T_path_total = T_clk - Slack_setup`, then compute `f_max = 1 / T_path_total`.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! Positive slack `+0.22 ns` means the critical path finished `0.22 ns` BEFORE the `1.923 ns` deadline (`1.923 - 0.22 = 1.703 ns`), allowing operation up to `1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz`!
Incorrect — Adding `+0.22 ns` corresponds to a NEGATIVE slack violation (`-0.22 ns`), whereas our slack is positive (`+0.22 ns`).
Incorrect — `0.22 ns` is the spare timing margin (slack), not the path delay.
Incorrect — Setup WNS directly determines the minimum safe clock period `T_clk,min` and therefore `f_max`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) Since `Slack_setup = T_clk - T_path_total = +0.22 ns`, the critical path takes `1.923 - 0.22 = 1.703 ns`, meaning the routed 14nm chip can run up to `1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz` even in the slowest `0.72V SS` corner!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (14nm Physical DRC Closure & M7 Clock Routing Rule)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 56 · 14nm Physical DRC & CTS Closure] Why did constraining Clock Tree Synthesis to metal layers `M2..M7` (`set_clock_routing_rules -net_type root -max_routing_layer M7`) eliminate the upper-metal DRC violations in standalone Synopsys IC Validator (`icv`)?
options: A) Because `M8` and `M9` are thick top-level power/global layers with wide minimum-spacing and fat-wire rules (`M8.S.6`, `M9.S.6`); keeping high-fanout clock tree branches on `M2..M7` avoids wide-metal stub spacing conflicts and achieves `0 / 242` DRC errors.
B) Because `M7` has zero electrical resistance.
C) Because `icv` only checks `M1`.
D) Because `M8` is made of polysilicon.
quiz_questions.hint: Compare the physical pitch and spacing rules of intermediate signal routing layers (`M2..M7`) versus top-level thick power/global distribution layers (`M8, M9`) in a 14nm FinFET BEOL stack.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! In `SAED14nm`, `M8/M9` carry the PG mesh straps and enforce wide-metal spacing rules (`M8.S.6`, `M9.S.6`). Restricting CTS to `M2..M7` eliminates all upper-metal stub conflicts (`0 / 242` DRC violations).
Incorrect — All copper metal layers have finite sheet resistance `R_s`.
Incorrect — Standalone `icv` evaluates all 242 foundry deck rules across FEOL (FinFET active/gate) and BEOL (`M1..M9` and vias).
Incorrect — `M8` is an upper back-end-of-line (BEOL) copper interconnect layer, not front-end polysilicon.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) Routing clock nets up to `M7` leaves `M8/M9` clean for power/top routing and resolves all 242 SAED14nm deck rules with `0` violations.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Midterm Q3/Q5/Q10 — Same-Edge Hold Physics Across PVT Corners)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 56 · Advanced Multi-Corner STA Physics] Suppose a classmate sees a Hold violation (`Hold WNS = -0.08 ns`) in PrimeTime at the `ff0p88v125c` (Fast-Fast `0.88V`) corner and proposes lowering the clock frequency from `520 MHz` (`1.923 ns`) down to `250 MHz` (`4.000 ns`) to fix it. Based on Midterm Q3 & Q10, will lowering `f_clk` fix the hold violation, and what is the true physical fix?
options: A) Yes, doubling the clock period adds `+2.077 ns` to Hold Slack.

B) No! Hold is checked on the SAME rising clock edge (`Slack_hold = [t_CQ,min + t_logic,min] - [t_hold,max + t_skew]`), which does NOT contain `T_clk`! Lowering frequency has zero effect on hold slack; the true fix is inserting non-inverting delay buffers (`set_fix_hold`) on the short contamination path to increase `t_logic,min` by >= `0.08 ns`.
C) Yes, because hold violations only happen above 500 MHz.
D) No, the only fix is deleting the flip-flop.
quiz_questions.hint: Write down the Hold Slack equation from Midterm Q3 / Q5 / Q10: does the clock period `T_clk` appear anywhere in `(t_CQ,min + t_logic,min) - (t_hold,max + t_skew)`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Adding `+2.077 ns` to `T_clk` increases SETUP slack by `+2.077 ns`, but changes HOLD slack by `0.000 ns`!

Correct! Because Hold checks that a launching DFF does not overwrite a capturing DFF on the SAME clock edge (`t = 0`), `T_clk` cancels out completely. Only adding minimum path delay (delay buffers via `set_fix_hold`) or reducing clock skew fixes a hold violation!
Incorrect — Even a `1 Hz` (`T_clk = 1 second`) clock will fail Hold if `t_CQ,min + t_logic,min < t_hold + t_skew` on the active clock edge!
Incorrect — Deleting pipeline flip-flops breaks the synchronous systolic architecture.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) Directly proven in Midterm Q3, Q5, and Q10: `Slack_hold = (t_CQ,min + t_logic,min) - (t_hold,max + t_skew)` is independent of `T_clk`. In Fusion Compiler / PrimeTime, `set_fix_hold` inserts small delay cells along fast paths (such as direct `Rpipe` shift wires) so `Slack_hold >= 0.00 ns` across all 3 corners.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 3 · Medium (Midterm Q3/Q4/Q9 — Setup Slack & F_max Math)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 57 · STA Setup & Hold Equations] Our 14nm Motion Estimator achieves Setup WNS = `+0.22 ns` in the worst-case slow corner (`ss0p72vm40c`) at `T_clk = 1.923 ns` (520 MHz). What is the longest critical-path total arrival + setup + uncertainty time in `ss0p72vm40c`, and what is the maximum achievable clock frequency?
options: A) Critical path total time = `1.923 ns - 0.22 ns = 1.703 ns`; max frequency `f_max = 1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz`.
B) Critical path total time = `1.923 ns + 0.22 ns = 2.143 ns`; max frequency = `466 MHz`.
C) Critical path total time = `0.22 ns`; max frequency = `4.5 GHz`.
D) Setup WNS does not affect maximum frequency.
quiz_questions.hint: Use the fundamental Setup Slack identity: `Slack_setup = T_clk - T_path_total`. Solve for `T_path_total = T_clk - Slack_setup`, then compute `f_max = 1 / T_path_total`.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! Positive slack `+0.22 ns` means the critical path finished `0.22 ns` BEFORE the `1.923 ns` deadline (`1.923 - 0.22 = 1.703 ns`), allowing operation up to `1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz`!
Incorrect — Adding `+0.22 ns` corresponds to a NEGATIVE slack violation (`-0.22 ns`), whereas our slack is positive (`+0.22 ns`).
Incorrect — `0.22 ns` is the spare timing margin (slack), not the path delay.
Incorrect — Setup WNS directly determines the minimum safe clock period `T_clk,min` and therefore `f_max`.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) Since `Slack_setup = T_clk - T_path_total = +0.22 ns`, the critical path takes `1.923 - 0.22 = 1.703 ns`, meaning the routed 14nm chip can run up to `1 / 1.703 ns = 587.2 MHz` even in the slowest `0.72V SS` corner!

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 4 · Hard (14nm Physical DRC Closure & M7 Clock Routing Rule)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 57 · 14nm Physical DRC & CTS Closure] Why did constraining Clock Tree Synthesis to metal layers `M2..M7` (`set_clock_routing_rules -net_type root -max_routing_layer M7`) eliminate the upper-metal DRC violations in standalone Synopsys IC Validator (`icv`)?
options: A) Because `M8` and `M9` are thick top-level power/global layers with wide minimum-spacing and fat-wire rules (`M8.S.6`, `M9.S.6`); keeping high-fanout clock tree branches on `M2..M7` avoids wide-metal stub spacing conflicts and achieves `0 / 242` DRC errors.
B) Because `M7` has zero electrical resistance.
C) Because `icv` only checks `M1`.
D) Because `M8` is made of polysilicon.
quiz_questions.hint: Compare the physical pitch and spacing rules of intermediate signal routing layers (`M2..M7`) versus top-level thick power/global distribution layers (`M8, M9`) in a 14nm FinFET BEOL stack.
choice_diagnostics: Correct! In `SAED14nm`, `M8/M9` carry the PG mesh straps and enforce wide-metal spacing rules (`M8.S.6`, `M9.S.6`). Restricting CTS to `M2..M7` eliminates all upper-metal stub conflicts (`0 / 242` DRC violations).
Incorrect — All copper metal layers have finite sheet resistance `R_s`.
Incorrect — Standalone `icv` evaluates all 242 foundry deck rules across FEOL (FinFET active/gate) and BEOL (`M1..M9` and vias).
Incorrect — `M8` is an upper back-end-of-line (BEOL) copper interconnect layer, not front-end polysilicon.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: A) Routing clock nets up to `M7` leaves `M8/M9` clean for power/top routing and resolves all 242 SAED14nm deck rules with `0` violations.

quiz_questions.difficulty_label: Level 5 · Advanced Challenge (Midterm Q3/Q5/Q10 — Same-Edge Hold Physics Across PVT Corners)
quiz_questions.q: [Page 57 · Advanced Multi-Corner STA Physics] Suppose a classmate sees a Hold violation (`Hold WNS = -0.08 ns`) in PrimeTime at the `ff0p88v125c` (Fast-Fast `0.88V`) corner and proposes lowering the clock frequency from `520 MHz` (`1.923 ns`) down to `250 MHz` (`4.000 ns`) to fix it. Based on Midterm Q3 & Q10, will lowering `f_clk` fix the hold violation, and what is the true physical fix?
options: A) Yes, doubling the clock period adds `+2.077 ns` to Hold Slack.

B) No! Hold is checked on the SAME rising clock edge (`Slack_hold = [t_CQ,min + t_logic,min] - [t_hold,max + t_skew]`), which does NOT contain `T_clk`! Lowering frequency has zero effect on hold slack; the true fix is inserting non-inverting delay buffers (`set_fix_hold`) on the short contamination path to increase `t_logic,min` by >= `0.08 ns`.
C) Yes, because hold violations only happen above 500 MHz.
D) No, the only fix is deleting the flip-flop.
quiz_questions.hint: Write down the Hold Slack equation from Midterm Q3 / Q5 / Q10: does the clock period `T_clk` appear anywhere in `(t_CQ,min + t_logic,min) - (t_hold,max + t_skew)`?
choice_diagnostics: Incorrect — Adding `+2.077 ns` to `T_clk` increases SETUP slack by `+2.077 ns`, but changes HOLD slack by `0.000 ns`!

Correct! Because Hold checks that a launching DFF does not overwrite a capturing DFF on the SAME clock edge (`t = 0`), `T_clk` cancels out completely. Only adding minimum path delay (delay buffers via `set_fix_hold`) or reducing clock skew fixes a hold violation!
Incorrect — Even a `1 Hz` (`T_clk = 1 second`) clock will fail Hold if `t_CQ,min + t_logic,min < t_hold + t_skew` on the active clock edge!
Incorrect — Deleting pipeline flip-flops breaks the synchronous systolic architecture.
quiz_questions.explain: Answer Key: B) Directly proven in Midterm Q3, Q5, and Q10: `Slack_hold = (t_CQ,min + t_logic,min) - (t_hold,max + t_skew)` is independent of `T_clk`. In Fusion Compiler / PrimeTime, `set_fix_hold` inserts small delay cells along fast paths (such as direct `Rpipe` shift wires) so `Slack_hold >= 0.00 ns` across all 3 corners.
